terms.x: Literally ‘sons of God’ or ‘sons of the gods.’ In Genesis 6, Job 1-2, Job 38, Psalm 29, and Psalm 89, the term refers to divine beings — members of the heavenly council. Not human beings. (Source: Heiser, The Unseen Realm.)
Hebrew term for ‘demons’ or hostile spirit beings. Appears in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37, where Israel is condemned for sacrificing to shedim rather than to Yahweh. (Source: Heiser, Walton)
The ‘council of El’ or ‘divine assembly.’ Appears in Psalm 82:1: ‘God stands in the divine assembly; in the midst of the gods He renders judgment.’ (Source: Heiser, The Unseen Realm.)

The personal, covenantal name of the God of Israel, revealed at the burning bush (Exodus 3). Often rendered ‘the LORD’ in English translations. The Tetragrammaton (YHWH) was held so sacred in Jewish tradition that it was not pronounced alou

Greek word commonly translated ‘servant’ in English New Testaments. More accurately means ‘slave’ or ‘bondservant.’ Paul opens several letters describing himself as a doulos of Christ — voluntarily owned, not merely employed. (Source: Wrigh

‘Slave of Christ.’ Paul’s self-identification in Romans 1:1, Philippians 1:1, Titus 1:1. A radical reframing of his identity under the kingship of Jesus, drawing on Old Testament ‘servant of Yahweh’ (eved Yahweh) language. (Source: Wright.)
Hebrew term for ‘servant’ or ‘slave.’ Used both for ordinary bondservice and for Israel’s relationship to Yahweh. Equivalent in semantic range to the Greek doulos.

‘Servant of Yahweh.’ Title applied in the Hebrew Bible to Moses, David, the prophets, and most famously to the figure described in Isaiah’s Servant Songs (Isaiah 42, 49, 50, 53). (Source: Wright, Old Testament theology.)

Hebrew word for ‘king.’ Used for human kings (Saul, David, the kings of Israel and Judah) and for Yahweh as cosmic king. The biblical theology of kingship traces from this term through the Davidic covenant to the New Testament’s identificat

Latin for ‘image of God.’ The theological concept, drawn from Genesis 1:26-27, that human beings are made in the image of God and therefore bear inherent dignity, moral responsibility, and representative function. (Source: Walton, Wright.)

Greek word meaning ‘word,’ ‘reason,’ or ‘principle.’ In John 1, the term identifies Jesus as the Logos — the eternal Word of God made flesh. Has a long pre-Christian philosophical history in Greek thought (Heraclitus, Stoicism). (Source: Wr

Aramaic term for ‘father.’ Used by Jesus in his prayer in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) and adopted by Paul to describe the believer’s intimate relationship with God (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). Not ‘daddy’ — a serious, relational address. (Sour
Greek for ‘the Father.’ Used throughout the New Testament, particularly in John’s Gospel and the Pauline epistles, of God as Father of Jesus and of believers through Christ.

Greek for ‘self-sufficient’ or ‘content.’ Paul uses this term in Philippians 4:11: ‘I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content (autarkēs).’ Carries a Stoic philosophical heritage that Paul reframes through Christ. (Source: Wright

Literally ‘the accuser’ or ‘the adversary.’ In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3, the term refers to a member of the heavenly council who functions as a prosecutor. The transition from ‘the adversary’ (a role) to ‘Satan’ (a personal name) develops ac

Hebrew term for the ‘giants’ or ‘fallen ones’ described in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33. Connected to the offspring of the union between the bene elohim and human women. (Source: Heiser, The Unseen Realm.)

Hebrew name for the realm of the dead. The shadowy underworld where all the dead were believed to go, prior to the developed eschatology of later Jewish and Christian thought. (Source: Heiser, Walton.)

A class of divine beings, mentioned in Daniel 4 and in extensive Second Temple Jewish literature (notably 1 Enoch). The Watchers tradition expands the Genesis 6 narrative of divine rebellion. Influential on the New Testament’s understanding

Hebrew term referring both to a giant clan in Canaan (Deuteronomy 2-3, Joshua 12) and to the spirits of the dead (Psalm 88:10, Isaiah 14:9). The dual meaning reflects ancient Near Eastern beliefs about the giant dead. (Source: Heiser.)
The ‘sons of Anak’ — a clan of giants encountered by the Israelite spies in Numbers 13. Connected in the biblical text to the Nephilim tradition. (Source: Heiser.)

Hebrew name for ‘Jacob’ — patriarch, son of Isaac, father of the twelve tribes of Israel. The name means ‘he grasps the heel’ or ‘supplanter,’ referring to Jacob’s birth and his early life of deception.

‘Yahweh of Hosts’ or ‘Yahweh of Armies.’ A divine title emphasizing Yahweh’s sovereignty over the heavenly armies — both spiritual beings and the cosmic order. … The Dictionary of Deities and Demons counts 284 occurrences of the title.

Ugaritic and Canaanite storm god, principal rival to Yahweh in the religious life of ancient Israel. Worship of Baal is repeatedly condemned in the prophets. The name means ‘lord’ or ‘master.’ (Source: Heiser)
Canaanite mother goddess, often paired with Baal in worship. Also refers to the wooden cult object associated with her. Frequently condemned in the Hebrew Bible. (Source: Walton, ANE background)
Living being, throat, appetite, life, self. Not a detachable ‘soul’ in the Greek sense — the whole breathing creature. Appears 754x.
Spirit, breath, wind. Used of God’s Spirit, the human spirit, and literal wind. Animating force.
Image. In Gen 1:26-27, humanity as God’s image — a status/office (representative function), not a physical resemblance.
Likeness. Paired with tselem in Gen 1:26. Reinforces the representative-function reading rather than physical copy.
Council, assembly, confidential circle. The ‘sod Yahweh’ (Jer 23:18, Ps 89:7) is the divine council where God deliberates with the heavenly host.
Heavens, sky. The dwelling realm of God and the heavenly host; also the visible sky.
Earth, land, ground. Often paired with shamayim as the merism for ‘all creation.’
Steadfast covenant love, loyal kindness, mercy. A core attribute of Yahweh’s character toward His people.
Covenant — a binding, often blood-sealed, relationship/agreement. The structural backbone of the OT (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic).
Instruction, teaching, law. The first five books; more broadly God’s directive guidance, not merely legal code.
Holiness, set-apartness. The quality of being dedicated/separated to Yahweh; the opposite of common (chol).
Glory, weight, honor. The manifest, weighty presence of Yahweh (the kavod filling the tabernacle/temple).
Peace, wholeness, completeness, welfare. Not mere absence of conflict but flourishing and right-order.
To sin, to miss the mark. The most common sin-word; a failure to hit the target of God’s standard.
Iniquity, guilt, the twistedness of sin and its consequence. Heavier than a single act — bent moral state.
Transgression, rebellion. Sin as willful revolt against authority, not just error.
Kinsman-redeemer. The relative obligated to buy back, avenge, or restore (Boaz; Yahweh as Israel’s goel).
Anointed one, Messiah. Originally any anointed king/priest; develops into the eschatological deliverer.
The Holy Spirit / Spirit of holiness. God’s empowering, set-apart presence.

“Burning ones,” from saraph, to burn. The six-winged beings of Isaiah’s throne-room vision, fiery serpentine guardians of the throne who function as members of the divine council (Isaiah 6:2; Revelation 4:8).
Throne-guardian beings (Gen 3:24; Ezekiel’s living creatures). Composite-form guardians of sacred space.
Messenger, angel. Function-word, not a species — a sent one, human or divine.
Day; period of time. The ‘days’ of Gen 1 — debated as 24-hr vs. epochs (relevant to old-earth reading).
‘Formless and void / unordered and empty’ (Gen 1:2). Describes the pre-ordered state creation is brought out of.
The deep, the primeval waters (Gen 1:2). Cognate to ANE chaos-waters; here de-mythologized under Yahweh.
Humanity / the man; wordplay with adamah (ground). Both a name and ‘humankind.’
Ground, soil, arable land. The stuff adam is formed from (Gen 2:7).
Flesh, body, kin, all living creatures. The physical/creaturely aspect of beings.
Heart — the seat of will, mind, and intention, not mainly emotion. The inner command-center of the person.
Faithfulness, steadfastness, reliability. Faith as enduring trustworthiness, not just mental assent.
Righteousness, justice. Right-relationship and right-order, both ethical and covenantal.
Justice, judgment, the right ruling. Often paired with tsedaqah as the social outworking of righteousness.
Word, thing, matter, event. A spoken word that accomplishes — God’s davar creates and acts.
Fear, reverence, awe. ‘The fear of Yahweh’ — reverent submission, the beginning of wisdom.
Wisdom — skilled living in alignment with the created order and God’s design. Central to Proverbs.
Assembly, congregation. The gathered people of Israel; LXX often renders it ekklesia.
Tabernacle, dwelling-place. The portable sanctuary where Yahweh’s presence ‘tents’ among Israel.
The ‘mercy seat’ / atonement-cover on the ark, where blood was applied on Yom Kippur.
To atone, cover, ransom, wipe away. The verb behind ‘atonement’ and Yom Kippur.
Age, long duration, eternity, the distant horizon of time. ‘Forever’ more as ‘far-off time’ than timelessness.
To touch, strike, reach. (Used in Ex 4:24-26 of Yahweh ‘meeting/touching’ Moses — a contested verb.)
Mighty one, warrior, hero. Used of human champions and of the Nephilim (‘mighty men of old’).
Helper, ally, strength. Used of the woman (Gen 2:18) and of God Himself — not a subordinate term.
God. In the NT, overwhelmingly the one God; the Greek term behind the OT elohim/Yahweh in the LXX.
Lord, master. Applied to Jesus; also the LXX’s standard rendering of YHWH — a deliberate identification.
Christ, Anointed One. Greek equivalent of mashiach/Messiah.
Spirit, breath, wind. The Holy Spirit, the human spirit, or wind — parallels Hebrew ruach.
Soul, life, self. Closer to Hebrew nephesh than to a Greek immortal-soul concept in NT usage.
Flesh. Physical body, but in Paul often the fallen, self-oriented human nature opposed to the Spirit.
Body. The whole physical person; for Paul, redeemable and destined for resurrection, not discarded.
Sin — ‘missing the mark.’ In Romans, not just acts but a personified power with agency operating through human nature.
Grace, favor, gift. Unmerited divine favor; the heart of Paul’s gospel.
Faith, faithfulness, trust, allegiance. Both belief and loyal trust — not mere intellectual assent.
Self-giving, willed love. The love that seeks the good of the other; God’s love and the command to imitate it.
Righteousness, justice. Both God’s covenant faithfulness and the right-standing given to believers.
To justify, declare righteous, set right. The verb at the center of the justification debate.
Repentance — a change of mind/direction. A turning, not merely feeling sorry.
Gospel, good news. In the 1st c., royal/imperial proclamation language — the announcement of a king’s accession.
Kingdom, reign, rule. ‘Kingdom of God’ as God’s active reign breaking in, more than a place.
Assembly, called-out gathering, church. A civic ‘assembly’ term, not originally a religious building.
Glory, honor, splendor. The NT counterpart to Hebrew kavod.
Holy, set apart, saint. Holiness language; ‘the saints’ = the set-apart people.
Salvation, deliverance, rescue, preservation. Broader than ‘going to heaven’ — rescue and wholeness.
Life. Especially ‘eternal life’ (zoe aionios) — the life of the age to come, qualitative not just unending.
Age, era, epoch. ‘This age’ vs. ‘the age to come’ — eschatological framing; behind ‘eternal’ (aionios).
World, ordered system. The created order, humanity, or the fallen world-system opposed to God.
Heaven, sky. The dwelling of God and the heavenly realm; parallels Hebrew shamayim.
Messenger, angel. Like Hebrew malak — function, a sent one, divine or human.
Demon, evil spirit. In the NT, hostile spiritual beings under the rebel powers; not the neutral Greek ‘daimon.’
Ruler, authority. Human officials and, in Paul, the hostile spiritual ‘rulers’ over the present age.
Authority, power, right. Delegated authority; in Paul also a class of spiritual ‘authorities/powers.’
Power, might, miracle. God’s power; the root of ‘dynamite’/’dynamic.’
Fear, reverence, terror. Ranges from terror to reverent awe (parallel to Hebrew yirah).
Wisdom. Skilled, God-aligned living; in 1 Cor, the wisdom of God vs. the wisdom of the world.
Truth, reality, what is unconcealed. For John, bound up with Christ Himself.
Peace. The NT counterpart to shalom — wholeness and reconciliation, not just calm.
Fellowship, partnership, sharing-in-common. Shared participation in Christ and with one another.
Covenant, will/testament. The Greek behind ‘New Covenant’ / ‘New Testament’; renders Hebrew berit.
Law. The Torah, or law/principle in general; central to Paul’s law-vs-grace argument.
Resurrection, a standing-up-again. Bodily resurrection, the hinge of Christian hope.
Arrival, presence, royal visit. The ‘coming’ of Christ — imperial-visit language.
Unveiling, revelation, disclosure. The title of Revelation; an uncovering of hidden reality.
Mystery — a previously hidden plan now revealed. Not a riddle but a disclosed secret (Paul’s ‘mystery’ of the gospel).
Advocate, helper, comforter, one called alongside. Used of the Spirit (and of Christ in 1 John).
Place/means of atonement, propitiation. The LXX word for the kapporet (mercy seat); applied to Christ in Rom 3:25.
To be moved with compassion ‘in the guts.’ Visceral, gut-level mercy — used of Jesus repeatedly.
Blessed, flourishing, fortunate. The ‘blessed’ of the Beatitudes — a state of God-favored flourishing.
Complete, mature, brought to its goal. ‘Perfect’ in the sense of finished/whole, not flawless.
To empty. The verb behind kenosis — Christ ’emptied himself’ (Phil 2:7); heavily debated in Christology.
Form, essential nature. ‘In the form of God’ (Phil 2:6) — the nature, not mere appearance.
One-of-a-kind, only-begotten, unique. Of Christ as the unique Son — ‘one and only’ rather than ‘created.’

Hebrew term for “gods” or “divine beings.” The Hebrew Bible uses it for Yahweh, for members of the divine council, for the gods of the nations, and occasionally for departed spirits. It is plural in form, and context sets its meaning more t
“The eye of a needle,” as Matthew words it in Matthew 19:24. Trypēma is a hole bored through something, a perforation, and rhaphis is an ordinary sewing needle.
“The eye of a needle,” as Mark words it in Mark 10:25. Trymalia is a hole or opening, and rhaphis is an ordinary sewing needle.
“The eye of a needle,” as Luke words it in Luke 18:25. Trēma is a hole or perforation, and belonē is a classical word for needle, possibly a surgical one.
Needle. A classical Attic word that Luke uses in Luke 18:25 in place of the everyday rhaphis. It may mean a surgical needle rather than a sewing one.
Camel. The word in all three Gospel versions of the needle saying (Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25, Luke 18:25), and the reading of the earliest manuscripts.
Rope, or a ship’s cable. One letter away from kamēlos, camel. A few late manuscripts of Matthew 19:24 and Luke 18:25 read it in place of camel, most likely a scribe softening the saying.
With difficulty, hardly. Jesus’s word in Matthew 19:23: a rich man will enter the kingdom with difficulty. Three verses later He raises it to adynaton, impossible.
Impossible. The neuter of adynatos, “without power.” Matthew 19:26: with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.

To hover or flutter. Used of the Spirit over the waters in Genesis 1:2 and of the eagle over its young in Deuteronomy 32:11. In its other stem, at Jeremiah 23:9, it means to tremble or grow soft. A verb of motion, not affection.
A Syriac verb from the same root as Hebrew rachaph. It can mean “to brood,” and it is the source of the brooding reading of Genesis 1:2.
“Was carried along over.” The Septuagint’s verb at Genesis 1:2 for the Spirit over the water, from epipherō, to bear upon. A verb of motion, with no sense of affection.
To yearn for, to long after. The Septuagint uses it at Deuteronomy 32:11 for the eagle over its young, where the Hebrew has rachaph. Paul uses it in Romans 1:11 and Philippians 1:8.
An Ugaritic verb, cognate with Hebrew rachaph, used of birds of prey soaring or hovering, including the goddess Anat in flight.
Womb. In the plural, rachamim, it becomes the Hebrew word for compassion and mercy. One consonant away from rachaph.
Formlessness, waste, emptiness. The “without form” of Genesis 1:2, and the “howling waste” where God finds Israel in Deuteronomy 32:10.
A wild ox, probably the aurochs, the huge wild bull now extinct. The King James Version renders it “unicorn” by way of the Septuagint’s monokerōs.
“One-horned.” The Septuagint’s rendering of the Hebrew re’em, which passed through the Latin unicornis into the King James “unicorn.”
Heart: the center of physical, mental, and spiritual life (Romans 2).
To boast, glory, or exult. In Romans 5 it describes boasting in the hope of God’s glory.
King (Judges 9).
Bramble or thorn-bush. It is the plant in Jotham’s parable (Judges 9).
Adoption: legal placement as a son (Romans 8).
Inheritance (Judges 1).
War (Judges 1).
Prophet.
Judge (Judges 3).
Victory.
Song.
To bless.
Sacrifice.
Army.
Fear.
Crown.
Snare.
Mercy or compassion.
Wings, and by extension protection.
Election, choice, or selection.
To repay, a term for legal compensation.
Notable person, or an acquaintance.
Salvation.
To harden, to make stubborn.
The grave, the Greek counterpart of Sheol.
End, goal, or fulfillment.

Abyss or bottomless pit. In Second Temple thought it is the prison of bound rebellious spirits (the Watchers of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch), opened in Revelation by a fallen star (Revelation 9:1-2, 11; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Luke 8:31).
Brother. The early church used it for fictive kinship, a claim of shared status in the household of God across class and ethnicity, which did not necessarily imply intimacy.
Without ceasing, literally “without leaving an interval.” Its sense of recurring rather than continuous action rests on ancient usage (a chronic cough, recurring attacks) (1 Thessalonians 5:17).
Let it alone: the vinedresser’s plea in the parable of the Barren Fig Tree (Luke 13:8). Snodgrass calls reading it as “forgive” an illegitimate totality transfer.
To exult or rejoice greatly. It belongs to Luke’s vocabulary of joy, as when Mary’s spirit rejoices (Luke 1:47).
Beloved. A higher-tier covenant term of address.
To praise, one of the core words in the Greek vocabulary of praise.
Ages. In Hebrews 11:3, Walton reads it as the ordering of the ages rather than the making of material creation.
Appointed lot, a portion dispensed by a god. It appears in a contested alternate etymology of diaita (dia plus aisa) proposed by Partridge and Klein.

Locust, its meaning everywhere in biblical Greek (plural akrides). John’s locusts were literal insects, kosher under Leviticus 11:22, and the carob “St. John’s bread” reading is later tradition (Mark 1:6; Matthew 3:4; Revelation 9:3).
Rooster. The word is unambiguous, and the cock crow at Peter’s denial was most likely a literal rooster (Mark 14:72).

Another. In “another angel” (Revelation 14:15) it places that angel alongside the three angels of verses 6 to 9 rather than the son of man. The subordination is one of function and says nothing about nature.

A doubled amen at the start of a sentence, found only in John (25 times) and rendered “verily, verily” in the KJV (John 3:3). Aune notes that introductory amen is attested but rare in Jewish literature.

A word of binding assent, carried untranslated from Hebrew: “I agree, and it binds me.” Like “aye” or “I do,” it attaches to what has just been said, so the people adopt it as their own (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; 1 Corinthians 14:16). Psalmists
Lamb: the other New Testament word for lamb, distinct from arnion (John 1:29, 36; Acts 8:32; 1 Peter 1:19).
Innumerable. Revelation sets the numbered 144,000 beside a multitude no one could number, echoing the promise to Abraham (Revelation 7:9; Genesis 15:5).

Shamelessness. In the parable of the friend at midnight (Luke 11:8), Bailey and Snodgrass both reject the translation “persistence.” Bailey assigns the shamelessness to the sleeper avoiding shame, and Snodgrass to the petitioner as a negati
To withstand. Together with “wisdom,” it is shared verbatim by Luke 21:15 and Acts 6:10, tying Jesus’ promise that adversaries could not withstand his followers to its fulfillment in Stephen.
Indefinite, unlimited. It is the source of the name of the aorist tense.

Meeting: the custom of citizens going out to meet an approaching dignitary and escorting him back into the city. Applied to 1 Thessalonians 4:17, the image is the church meeting Christ and returning with him (see also Matthew 25:6; Acts 28:
The preposition “from,” which takes the genitive case. That is why ho ōn in the nominative after it in Revelation 1:4 is a deliberate grammatical irregularity (a solecism).

Obscure, doubtful, secret, or hidden: that which lies outside the canon. In the ancient sense apocryphal did not mean heretical, and some Gnostics used the word to describe their own secret literature.
Radiance (Hebrews 1:3). Its only other ancient occurrence is in an apocryphal book.
Destruction, along with the waste of what could have been (Matthew 7:13).
Destroyer: the Greek name of the king of the abyss (Revelation 9:11). It plausibly puns on Apollo, a god of the imperial cult, unmasking the emperor’s god as the destroyer.
To defend oneself, specifically in the wording of a legal defense (Luke 21:14; 12:11).
Defense speech. Luke 21:14 says not to rehearse one, and 1 Peter 3:15 says always be ready with one: the same word in the same setting (see also Philippians 1:17).
To lose, perish, or destroy. “That nothing may be lost” (John 6:12) links to John 6:39, 17:12, and 3:16, where the concern is people rather than bread.

Wormwood, a bitter plant. In the Old Testament it is a metaphor for bitter judgment and the poisoned fruit of apostasy, which argues against reading it as a coded modern event such as Chernobyl (Revelation 8:11; Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Deuter
Rule. Paul uses it for a class of spiritual beings in the heavenly realm (Ephesians 1:21; 6:12).
Lamb: Revelation’s word, used 29 times and always of Jesus except in 13:11. It carries several meanings at once: sacrificial victim, servant, and conquering ruler (Revelation 5:6).
Literally “not slipping”: secure footing (Luke 1:4). Wright prefers “reliability” to “certainty,” since the point is that the ground is trustworthy, whatever the believer’s emotional state.
Bread. The barley loaves in John 6:9 are the bread of the poor, echoing Elisha’s miracle (2 Kings 4:42-44).
Star. In Revelation it can denote a supernatural being, one of the heavenly host or a fallen angel, as with the star given the key to the abyss (Revelation 9:1; 1:20; 12:4; Job 38:7).
Eyewitness (plural autoptai), literally a “self-seer” and the root of “autopsy.” Luke’s use of it places his Gospel within Hellenistic history-writing (Luke 1:2).
King of kings (Revelation 19:16). It is a cosmic claim that every authority, visible and invisible, including the elohim, is subordinate to Christ.

An old title of the Canaanite god Baal (Ugaritic zbl, “Prince” or “exalted Baal”) that by the first century had become a name for the ruler of the demons. In Mark 3:22 the accusation files Jesus under the enemy’s chain of command.

Little scroll, a diminutive of biblion. It is the open commissioning scroll John eats, in the manner of Ezekiel 2 and 3, and is likely distinct from the sealed scroll of chapter 5 (Revelation 10:2, 9-10; Ezekiel 2:8-3:3).
Book or scroll. In Revelation 5:1 the sealed scroll is written inside and on the back, most likely a rolled scroll written on both sides (an opisthograph).
Ancient Greco-Roman biography, which arranged events by theological or moral purpose and was selective rather than exhaustive. It is the genre of the Gospels (John 21:25).
Thunders, associated with the voice of God (Psalm 29). The utterance of the seven thunders was deliberately sealed and never written, so there is nothing to decode (Revelation 10:3-4).

Injurious speech: slander, reviling, defaming, attacking someone’s honor with words. It was an ordinary, non-religious word, and English transliterated it as “blasphemy” only for uses directed at God (Mark 3:28-30; Romans 2:24; Matthew 15:1
Decans (from deka, ten): astral powers each ruling 10 degrees of the zodiac. Egypt and Babylon counted 36, shifting to a 12 or 24 division in the Hellenistic period.
Wax tablets, the standard ancient notebook.
To bind. It is the root of doulos, slave.
Second law: the source of the name Deuteronomy, though the book reads better as Moses’s farewell sermons.
The slanderer. It is a title, like tempter and evil one.
Diadem, a sign of royal authority in the narrow sense. John avoids this word for the crowns of believers (Revelation 12:3; 13:1).
To separate or select (from dia, “apart,” and ainysthai, “to take”). It is the older layer beneath diaita.

Way of life or regimen, the source of the English “diet.” It comes from diaitan, originally “to separate, select, take apart,” which maps onto the Hebrew badal (Leviticus 20:25). An alternate etymology from dia plus aisa is speculative.
To lead one’s life.
Greek dietetics: a holistic approach to health and prevention that covered far more than what one ate.

Teaching: the title of The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, a 16-chapter church manual from the late first or early second century on morality, baptism, fasting, prayer, the Eucharist, and leadership. Lost for 18 centuries, it was rediscove
Dialect. The Testament of Job consistently uses it for angelic speech, whereas Paul uses glōssa, which weakens the proposed parallel with tongues.
Narrative, an ordered account (Luke 1:1).

Righteous. The Septuagint uses it to translate Hebrew tsaddiq, and it describes Noah, Abraham, and Job. Applied to Zechariah and Elizabeth, it marks them as first-rank covenant keepers (Luke 1:6; 23:47).
Will cut in two: the fate of the unfaithful servant (Matthew 24:51; Luke 12:46). Susanna 55 and 59 offer a parallel, where the angel waits with his sword to split the guilty in two.
To seem. It is the root of Docetism, the teaching that Jesus only seemed to have a body.
Female slave or bondservant, the feminine of doulos. It is Mary’s description of herself (Luke 1:38).
Veneration given to saints, which Catholic teaching distinguishes from latria (worship). Huff argues the distinction collapses in practice.
Honey cake. It sits behind a one-letter mistranslation theory (egkrides for akrides) used to argue that John the Baptist was vegetarian (Mark 1:6).

Dragon: the Old Testament chaos monster (Leviathan, Rahab) symbolizing evil kingdoms, especially Egypt, defeated as a sea dragon at the Exodus. Revelation 12:9 explicitly identifies it as the devil (Revelation 12:3, 9).

I am. In John 8:58 Jesus uses a timeless present set against Abraham’s coming into being, and the crowd’s attempt to stone him shows they heard a claim to the divine name (John 8:58-59; compare Exodus 3:14).

Meat sacrificed to an idol. Witherington reads it as meat eaten in the idol’s presence or temple, a form of ritual participation and the sin of Balaam, distinct from the marketplace meat Paul allows (Revelation 2:14, 20; 1 Corinthians 8 to
To enter. It is what the many do through the wide gate, set against the few who find (heuriskō) the narrow road (Matthew 7:13).
From, out of. In Revelation 3:10 (“keep you from the hour of trial”) it is contested whether it means removal from the trial or preservation through it (compare John 17:15).
“They sat.” A third-person plural aorist with no stated subject, an impersonal Semitic idiom that points back to the unnamed enthroned council of Daniel 7 (Revelation 20:4; Daniel 7:9).
A way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). It is paired with temptation and is not a promise that suffering will be limited.
A strong word of indignation, even snorting anger. It describes Jesus at Lazarus’s tomb, where many translations soften it to “deeply moved” (John 11:33).
A publishing term, used by Irenaeus (as quoted by Eusebius) of the release of Luke’s Gospel.

The word behind “daily” bread in the Lord’s Prayer, found almost nowhere else. Proposed meanings include “daily,” “for tomorrow” (an end-times reading), and Jerome’s “supersubstantial,” from epi plus a form related to ousia, “being” (Matthe

To overshadow. It is used of the Spirit overshadowing Mary, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud over the tabernacle and that appears at the Transfiguration, so Mary’s body becomes a kind of tabernacle (Luke 1:35; 9:34;
“On this rock” (Matthew 16:18). Following Augustine, the rock is read as Christ or Peter’s confession rather than Peter’s person.
“Coming,” or “the one who is to come.” It is the forward-looking third clause of the divine title in Revelation (Revelation 1:4, 8).
A Greek word for love, alongside agapē.
“Tabernacled,” or pitched a tent. The Word dwelt among us as the temple presence (John 1:14).
To give thanks. It is the source of the eucharistic overtone some see in John’s feeding story and bread discourse, a reading that is debated (John 6:11).
To bring or announce good news. It is the verb form of euangelion, a word used in imperial Roman propaganda before it became a Christian technical term (Luke 1:19).
Thanksgiving, and the name of the Eucharist. Outsiders misread talk of eating a body and drinking blood as cannibalism (Luke 22:19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26).
Broad, spacious, describing the road. It occurs only here in the New Testament and is paired with plateia, the broad gate (Matthew 7:13).
Immediately. It is Mark’s signature pacing word, often in the phrase kai euthys, “and immediately,” and it contrasts with Luke’s orderly account.
To buy back, redeem. It sits under “making the most of the time,” implying that time is actively being used up (Ephesians 5:16).
To deceive. It is the verb in “sin deceived me,” the same one Paul uses of the serpent deceiving Eve, so Romans 7 reads through Genesis 3 (Romans 7:11; 2 Corinthians 11:3).
“I led out.” The Greek Old Testament uses it in the prologue to the Ten Commandments, and it is related to exodos (Exodus 20:2).
“They were astonished.” The disciples’ astonishment shows that Jesus meant an impossibility, not merely a hard gate (Matthew 19:25).

Sorcery. In the New Testament it is chiefly about illicit power and allegiance, the imperial and economic machinery for seducing nations, rather than drugs, and it follows from idolatry (Galatians 5:20; Revelation 9:21; 18:23).
The classical root word, covering drug, remedy, poison and spell with no clear line between them.
A sorcerer, the agent noun of the pharmakon family (Revelation 21:8; 22:15).
To carry along, as a ship is carried by the wind. Peter says the prophets spoke as they were “carried along” by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:20-21).

A bowl, specifically a libation bowl used in temple offerings. In the Old Testament such bowls carried ashes and fat out of sacred space, so pouring them out suggests purifying the earth (Revelation 15:7; 16:1).
Friendship love. One argument holds that modern American culture has cut male friendship off, and the church has cut out its manliness, a “double amputation.”
Friend, a warm, second-tier term of address (John 15:15).
Light-bearer. It was the common Greek name for the planet Venus (as in Cicero), and 2 Peter 1:19 uses it for the morning star rising in the heart.
God-fearer: a Gentile attached to the synagogue who worshiped Israel’s God without full conversion (Acts 10).
Land, earth. It is the narrower word Paul does not use in Romans 4:13, where he says Abraham would inherit the kosmos, the world.

Gehenna, the Greek form of the Hebrew gê-hinnōm. It is Jesus’ term for the destiny of the wicked, absent from the Greek Old Testament and Josephus, and equivalent to the lake of fire. Later rabbis made it temporary (Matthew 25:41; Revelatio
“May it be.” It is one of four ways the Greek Old Testament renders Hebrew amen, and the Latin Vulgate follows with fiat.
“Kinds of tongues,” one of the spiritual gifts Paul lists (1 Corinthians 12:10).

terms.t: genoito moi kata to rhēma sou
terms.tr: genoito moi kata to rhēma sou
terms.x: “Let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). This is Mary’s fiat, consent given before understanding, which Wright takes as the mark of the first real disciple.
Giants. It is the Greek Old Testament rendering at Numbers 13:33, but that translation renders gibborim and rephaim inconsistently elsewhere, so it settles less than it seems (Genesis 6:4).
Knowledge. In Gnosticism it meant secret saving knowledge available only to a spiritual elite.
Writing, Scripture. It is the standard New Testament word for Scripture, marking written authority as distinct from oral teaching (2 Timothy 3:16).
Tongue, meaning both the body part and a language. The New Testament uses it for speaking in tongues and has no other technical term for the practice (Acts 2:4; 1 Corinthians 12 to 14).
Holy ones, saints. It is a standard name for the church and appears 13 times in Revelation after 4:1, which undercuts the argument that the church is absent from those chapters.

Blood. In Revelation it always stands for the suffering of the wicked or of Christ and the saints, which supports reading the second and third bowls as judgment on people rather than on water (Revelation 16:3-6).
To rejoice. It is part of what makes Luke the gospel of joy (Luke 1:14).

A mark or stamp, like an imperial stamp. The mark of Revelation 13 signals allegiance and ownership, “the name of the beast,” as the counterpart to the seal (sphragizō) of chapter 7 (Revelation 13:16-17; 14:11).
To bestow grace or favor. Its perfect passive participle gives Mary’s title “favored one” (Luke 1:28).

To catch up, seize. “We shall be caught up” in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 comes with a trumpet and a shout, so the event is public, not secret. The catching up is in the text, the modern pre-tribulation system is not (Matthew 13:19; Acts 8:39; 2
Armageddon. Heiser (The Unseen Realm) reads it as har-moʿed, the mount of assembly, meaning Zion, where the nations march, rather than Megiddo (Revelation 16:16).

The first resurrection: the general resurrection the Old Testament anticipated (Daniel 12). Those raised rule with the Messiah after Armageddon, and no “second resurrection” is ever named (Revelation 20:5-6).
The day of the Lord in the Greek Old Testament, a period of end-times judgment and vindication. It is distinct from kyriakē hēmera, the Lord’s day, in Revelation 1:10.
“Seven mountains,” the seven hills of Rome, which decode the beast’s seven heads (Revelation 17:9).
Dawn-bringer, morning star. It is the Greek Old Testament rendering of Hebrew helel in Isaiah 14:12, standing between the Hebrew and the Latin lucifer.
To interpret or explain. It is linked to Hermes, the messenger god who carried meaning between the divine and human worlds.
“Other tongues.” Luke’s phrase at Pentecost presents them as real, understandable human languages (Acts 2:4).
To find. “Few find it” (Matthew 7:14) uses the same verb as “seek and you will find” (Matthew 7:7), so the road is searched for, not stumbled into.
A thousand. It is the root of “chiliasm,” the Greek-based equivalent of the Latin-based “millennialism” (Revelation 20).
A Greek conjunction of purpose or result, “so that.” It introduces the clause about the man of God being fully equipped (2 Timothy 3:17).
“Beyond our strength” (2 Corinthians 1:8-9). Paul was burdened beyond his ability, which contradicts the saying that God never gives you more than you can handle.
The single subject or person of Christ as defined at Chalcedon, set against Babai’s two qnōmē.
Pale, pale green. Normally the green of plants, here it is the sickly pallor of a corpse on the horse named Death, and “pale” undersells it (Revelation 6:8).
The second death: final judgment and final dying, defined by Revelation 20:15 as the lake of fire (Revelation 20:6, 14; 21:8).
The slanderer, the accuser. It is the Greek Old Testament rendering of ha-satan, keeping both the article and the role.
“The Word of God,” the name of the rider in Revelation 19. He is the returning Christ, whose sword from his mouth strikes the nations (Revelation 19:13).
“Those who dwell on the earth.” It is Revelation’s stock phrase for the unbelieving, idolatrous world that receives the woes (Revelation 3:10; 6:10; 8:13; 13:8).

terms.t: ho mathētēs hon ēgapa ho Iēsous
terms.tr: ho mathētēs hon ēgapa ho Iēsous
terms.x: “The disciple whom Jesus loved.” The definite article singles out one person, a reverent self-concealment rather than arrogance, and John 21:24 names him as the Gospel’s author or source (John 13:23).
Of the same substance. It was Nicaea’s answer to Arius: the Son is of the same substance as the Father, not merely like him.

“The One Who Is,” the Greek Old Testament form of the divine name in Exodus 3:14. Revelation 1:4 keeps it in an ungrammatical nominative as a signal, and Philo also uses it as a divine name (Revelation 1:8).
Because. In Mark 3:30 it connects the teaching on the unforgivable sin to everything before it, tying it to the scribes’ accusation (Bratcher and Nida).
The title meaning Messiah, “anointed one.” Tacitus mistakenly treats it as a personal name.
“There will be no more delay.” Daniel’s deferral and the martyrs’ “wait a little longer” are over, and the phrase does not claim that time itself ends (Revelation 10:6; Daniel 12:7; Revelation 6:11).
Most High. It is the Greek Old Testament rendering of Hebrew Elyon, and in pagan Greek a title of Zeus, which lies behind the anti-Zeus reading of Revelation 1:4 (Luke 1:32, 35, 76).
“Behold, the slave of the Lord” (Luke 1:38). Mary’s word doulē is the strongest term of submission and the model of discipleship.
Jasper, a stone tied to God’s dwelling place in the new Jerusalem, the tabernacle, and Eden (Revelation 4:3; Genesis 2:12).
“And so we are” (1 John 3:1). A scribe’s eye skipped from the -men ending of klēthōmen to the -men of esmen, dropping the phrase, which is why the KJV omits it.
Literally a measuring rod. It came to mean “the standard,” then “the authoritative list”: the closed list of books recognized as divinely inspired Scripture.
According to. It is the formula in the Gospel titles (kata Markon, “according to Mark”), a label added by librarians or scribes rather than an author’s signature.
Guest room, not inn. There was no heartless innkeeper: Jesus was born in a crowded family home, and the point is lowliness, not loneliness (Luke 2:7; 22:11).
To pass away, be done away with. Paul uses it for prophecy and knowledge in 1 Corinthians 13:8.
To instruct orally, to catechize. Theophilus had been instructed this way but needed a written foundation (Luke 1:4).
Orderly, in sequence. Luke’s “orderly account” need not mean strict chronology and can include thematic and theological ordering (Luke 1:3).
“Favored one,” the perfect passive of charitoō. Mary is graced by God’s choosing, not filled with an inner quality. The Vulgate’s “full of grace” underlies Catholic teaching on Mary (Luke 1:28).
Horned. It is Aquila’s rendering of the Hebrew word describing Moses’ face in Exodus 34:29, which Jerome followed.
Proclamation: the oral preaching about Jesus before and alongside the written Gospels.
An ancient Mediterranean ritual drink. Muraresku argues it was psychedelic, a claim critics call overreach.
The Lord’s day (Revelation 1:10), most likely Sunday, the resurrection day, not the Sabbath. It is distinct from the Greek Old Testament’s hēmera tou kyriou, the end-times day of the Lord.
Dominion. Paul uses it as a term for spiritual powers (Ephesians 1:21; Colossians 1:16).
The breaking of bread, a full shared meal (an agape feast) rather than a token ritual (Acts 2:42).
Basket. The twelve baskets of leftovers stand for the twelve tribes, all Israel gathered with none lost (John 6:13).
The common Greek language of the Roman world, part of the “fullness of time” that prepared the way for the gospel mission (Galatians 4:4).
World rulers of darkness. They are read as the disinherited divine beings of Deuteronomy 32 against whom the church wars (Ephesians 6:12).
Partner, sharer. It is a higher-tier covenant term of address.

Most excellent, a formal title (kratiste when addressing someone) used of the Roman officials Felix and Festus. Its use for Theophilus suggests he was a real person of high status (Luke 1:3; Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25).
Worship due to God alone, contrasted with dulia (veneration).
Usually ‘thieves’ or ‘robbers’, but the word connotes violent insurrectionists. It is used of the men crucified with Jesus.

“White.” Sixteen of its 26 New Testament uses are in Revelation, where it is the color of the heavenly realm and of faithful believers, and being made white signals membership in the divine council (Revelation 3:4-5, 18; Daniel 12:10).
Matthew’s plural, unnumbered term for the visitors from the east (Matthew 2:1). The traditional number ‘three’ was inferred from the three gifts.

To be anxious, ordinary anxious care, as in “do not be anxious” (Matthew 10:19; Luke 12:11). It is the same verb as Matthew 6:25, and it forbids anxiety, while study and preparation are left untouched.
“Between rivers”: the land between the Tigris and Euphrates.
“Midheaven,” the zenith over the earth (Revelation 14:6). It presupposes a premodern flat-disc cosmology, a point from which all could hear.
The Orthodox term for the real change of the Eucharistic elements, affirmed as dogma at the Synod of Jerusalem (1672).
Forehead, the place of the beast’s mark (Revelation 13:16).

“One hour”: the brief reign allotted to the ten kings, and the swiftness of Babylon’s judgment (Revelation 17:12; 18:10, 17, 19). It echoes Daniel 4:17 in the Septuagint, Nebuchadnezzar’s beast period.
“Myriads of myriads,” an idiom for an innumerable host (Revelation 9:16; 5:11). The host is angelic in Daniel 7:10 and demonic in Revelation 9, and the phrase is not a literal troop count.
“Foolishness,” the source of English “moronic.” It is what Christ crucified was to the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).
“Temple” or “sanctuary.” In the new Jerusalem “its temple is the Lord God and the Lamb”: God’s presence, once sequestered in the holy of holies, now fills the whole city (Revelation 21:22).

“Temple of God,” a phrase at the center of the debate over dating Revelation (Revelation 11:1). It is qualified as “in heaven” only at 11:19, which raises the question of an earthly versus a heavenly temple.
“To conquer” or “overcome” (Revelation 5:5). It frames Christ’s atoning death as victory over evil powers (compare nikos in 1 Corinthians 15:54 and John 16:33), without excluding substitution.
“House” or “household of God.” In 1 Timothy 3:15 it means God’s people or family, and the New Testament never uses it of a building.
A scroll written on both sides, fitting the description “within and on the back” (Revelation 5:1; Ezekiel 2:9-10).
To cut a path or stone straight. Found only in 2 Timothy 2:15, where it describes exactness and precision in handling the word of truth.
“Reproach,” a strong shame word. Luke uses it for Elizabeth’s decades of public disgrace in an honor-shame culture (Luke 1:25).
Being or substance. Its root is linked to epiousios (the “daily” bread of the Lord’s Prayer), and the same term is central to Trinitarian theology.
Parable. The word never appears in John, so John has no parables in the Synoptic sense.
A commercial inn, the one used in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:34).
To hand over or deliver. It is used in Satan’s claim that authority “has been delivered to me” (Luke 4:6) and of Judas’s betrayal.
Sojourner or resident alien, a term used in 1 Peter for believers (1 Peter 2:11).
“Tradition,” what is handed down. It describes how New Testament material was transmitted before being written (1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15).
Simple “and … and …” sentence linking, characteristic of Mark’s rough Greek.
Figure of speech or proverb. It is John’s term for sayings like the Good Shepherd and the Vine (John 10:6; 16:25, 29), distinct from the Synoptic parables.
‘Cease’ in the middle voice, used of tongues in 1 Corinthians 13:8. Its difference from katargeō in the same verse is stylistic and cannot bear cessationist weight.
Passover. The KJV renders it ‘Easter’ once, a translation artifact often cited against KJV-only doctrine.
Temptation or testing. In 1 Corinthians 10:13 the subject is temptation and a way of escape, so the saying ‘God won’t give you more than you can handle’ misreads the verse.
To persuade or convince. It is the root of pistis: faith as being persuaded enough to entrust yourself.
An odd Greek transliteration of the divine name found in some Septuagint manuscripts. The Greek capitals visually mimic the Hebrew letters YHWH.
“Fire.” It is the root of Purouel, the archangel of fire in the Testament of Abraham who tests people’s works by fire (Revelation 14:18).
A debated phrase: ‘faith in Christ’ or ‘the faithfulness of Christ.’ Bates argues for ‘allegiance.’

“To lead astray” or “deceive” (BDAG: leading astray in a specific way). In Revelation 20:3 it is defined by what Satan does when released: leading the nations against Zion, instigating Armageddon (compare Revelation 12:9).
To fulfill or complete. It carries the reading that Jesus came to complete the law, not cancel it (Matthew 5:17).
“Broad, wide,” the word describing the wide gate (Matthew 7:13).
“Fullness of time,” Paul’s phrase for the providential moment of Jesus’ birth (Galatians 4:4).

‘Unclean spirit,’ the common New Testament exorcism term (Mark 1:23; 5:2), found once in the Old Testament (Zechariah 13:2) and 21 times in the New. It is interchangeable with ‘evil spirit’ or ‘demon,’ and ‘unclean’ is ambiguous between mor

“Seducing” or “deceiving spirits,” Paul’s term for the spirits behind false teaching, paired with “doctrines of demons” (1 Timothy 4:1, where the form is pneumasin planois). The phrase has been wrongly chained with “unclean spirits” and “fa
Spiritual, a Spirit-person. In 1 Corinthians 12 every member is gifted by the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7).
“Of many turns,” the epithet for Odysseus’s cunning.
“Many.” Luke admits that many have already compiled narratives, possibly Mark, Q, and Matthew (Luke 1:1). It is historiographical modesty rather than polemic.

“Prostitute” or “harlot,” the Old Testament metaphor for idolatry (Revelation 17:1, 5). It is applied to seducer empires such as Nineveh, Tyre, and Babylon (Nahum 3:4; Isaiah 23:17), while seduced Israel is pictured instead as an unfaithful
Meek (Matthew 5:5; 11:29). The picture is a war horse broken to the bridle: power under authority, not weakness.
‘Falling headlong’ (Acts 1:18). Some translators (Phillips, Moffatt, Goodspeed) propose a medical sense, ‘swelling up.’
‘Having become swollen,’ a proposed reading of Acts 1:18 reflected in later Syriac, Georgian, and Armenian manuscripts.
“Elder,” the word for the elders around the throne in Revelation 4:4. In Mediterranean inscriptions it is synonymous with dekanos (decan), which Malina uses as the hook for an astral reading.

‘Prophets’ (Luke 24:44). In the Delphi parallel sometimes drawn to tongues, the prophētai were oracle officials alleged to translate the Pythia’s utterances. Forbes argues they were officials, not translators of gibberish.
A classical rhetorical term for rehearsing a declamation. Luke 21:14 forbids drafting the courtroom speech in advance, while knowing Scripture is still expected.
A later compound meaning “be anxious in advance” (Mark 13:11). It points to anxiety beforehand rather than preparation beforehand (Robertson).
To bow down or prostrate oneself in worship, the kneeling posture of biblical praise.
‘Person’ or ‘face.’ For Rome and Alexandria it meant an individual subject, while the Syriac equivalent parsopa meant ‘appearance in a nature,’ a key source of confusion behind the ‘Nestorian’ label.
“Patron,” Phoebe’s title in relation to Paul (Romans 16:1-2).
“Psalms,” the third division of Scripture named in Luke 24:44, standing for the Writings.
A pebble or stone, a gem, or a voting stone, hence a “vote.” A white stone meant acquittal or a favorable vote (Revelation 2:17).
The archangel “of fire” in the Testament of Abraham who tests works by fire. He forms background for the angel with authority over fire (Revelation 14:18).
Needle, the word in Matthew 19:24 and Mark 10:25. The Gospels use differing words for needle, which shows the saying does not name a gate.
“Trumpet,” corresponding to the shofar. It signals theophany, alarm, and holy war (Revelation 8:2, 6; Exodus 19; Joel 2:1; Joshua 6).
Word, utterance, spoken message, as in Mary’s response: “according to your word” (Luke 1:38).
“Carnelian,” a stone associated with the divine abode (Revelation 4:3).
“Worshiper,” an alternate term for a God-fearer.
Sign. John frames the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing beyond itself toward the Bread of Life discourse (John 6:14).
“Seal,” the mark of God’s ownership on believers (Revelation 7). The beast’s charagma is its dark mirror (Revelation 13:16).

To seal. The seal on the forehead marks ownership and protection with the name of the Lamb and the Father, protecting from God’s wrath rather than from physical suffering (Revelation 7:3-4; 14:1). It parallels the beast’s charagma, which po
The sycamore fig Zacchaeus climbs (Luke 19:4). The tree is characteristic of Jericho and not of Italy, Greece, or Turkey, a checkable local detail Luke gets right.
“Silence,” the loaded silence of the seventh seal before Day of the Lord judgment, in which the saints’ prayers rise (Revelation 8:1; Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:13).
“Co-laborer” or “fellow worker,” a New Testament term of address for partners in ministry.
Tent. James quotes David’s fallen tent (Amos 9:11-12) at the Jerusalem Council to justify Gentile inclusion (Acts 15:16).
“To tabernacle” or “dwell,” the verb of Revelation 21:3. It is the same verb as John 1:14 (the Word tabernacled among us), pointing to the body of Christ as God’s dwelling.
“Emerald,” the appearance of the rainbow around the throne (Revelation 4:3).
A grammatical mistake. In Revelation these are intentional “grammatical howlers” that signal a Hebrew or Septuagint source, since John “writes in Greek but thinks in Hebrew” (Revelation 1:4).

The low stone barrier in Herod’s temple that excluded Gentiles on pain of death. Paul invokes it as the “dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), and it lies behind the outer court given to the nations (Revelation 11:2).
Save, heal, make whole. Using it to claim guaranteed physical healing in the atonement is a word-study fallacy, since 1 Peter 2:24 and Isaiah 53:5 point to spiritual healing.
“Savior,” a title officially used of Augustus. Luke applies it to Jesus (Luke 2:11).
“Narrow,” of the narrow gate (Matthew 7:13-14). It is a size word and gives English “stenosis.”
“Elements” (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:8, 20). Alderink, in the Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, reaches the “powers” sense through the elements reading.
Family affection, one of the Greek words for love alongside agapē. It does not appear in the New Testament.
‘Same body,’ fellow members of one body: Gentiles as fellow heirs (Ephesians 3:6).
“Fellow soldier,” a covenant term of address (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 2).
‘The prayers’: corporate and probably liturgically structured prayer (Acts 2:42).
“Titan,” Irenaeus’s preferred solution to 666 (T300 + E5 + I10 + T300 + A1 + N50 = 666). It is speculatively linked to the Giants, Nimrod, and Babel (Revelation 13:18).
The underworld prison where the sinning angels, the Watchers, are held. It is the mechanism behind the “spirits in prison” (2 Peter 2:4; 1 Peter 3:19).
‘To cast into Tartarus,’ the Greek prison of the rebellious Titans. It is used of the angels who sinned (2 Peter 2:4).
Tax collector. Matthew’s role required bilingual literacy, the strongest educational case among the Gospel authors (Matthew 9:9).
Pressed, constricted. The perfect passive participle of thlibō, used of the narrow road in Matthew 7:14: it describes force more than size, a way that presses and brings trouble (BDAG).

Sea of glass. It pictures chaos calmed and mastered: the Red Sea of a new Exodus joined with the firmament under God’s throne in Ezekiel 1 (Revelation 15:2; Ezekiel 1:22). The sea is abolished in Revelation 21:1.
To marvel or be astonished. Jesus marvels only at the centurion’s faith and at Israel’s unbelief (Matthew 8:10; Mark 6:6).
Foundation. Luke’s parable of the Two Builders has a single foundation laid on rock (Luke 6:48), which Snodgrass says does not allude to Isaiah 28:16.
God-taught. The word appears to be Paul’s coinage, applied to Jewish and Gentile believers taught by God through the proclamation of the cross (1 Thessalonians 4:9; compare John 6:45).
Lover or friend of God, from theos (God) and philos (friend). The honorific in Luke 1:3 suggests a real patron of high status, with a secondary resonance for every reader.
God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16). Scripture is breathed out the way breath carries words, so the words are God’s while the authors remain genuinely human.
God-bearer, a stronger claim than Christ-bearer. The title for Mary was affirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431.
Beast or wild animal. Revelation uses it for both of its beasts (Revelation 13:1, 11), and the Septuagint uses it for Job’s land beast, Behemoth.
To press together or constrict. It is the root of tethlimmenē and thlipsis (Matthew 7:14; 2 Corinthians 4:8).
Affliction or pressure, the standard New Testament word for being pressed. It is used of the crowd pressing on Jesus and of being “pressed on every side” (Mark 3:9; 2 Corinthians 4:8; Matthew 7:14).
Religion as outward worship. James 1:26 calls religion without a bridled tongue worthless, and James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows and staying unstained by the world.
Throne. The definite article in Revelation 2:13 points to a specific, recognizable throne of imperial and pagan power.
The Greek numerals for 318: T (300) stands for the cross and IH (18) for the first letters of Iēsous. Barnabas uses it as a cross typology of Abraham’s 318 men (Genesis 14:14).
The Amen. Paul’s phrase in 1 Corinthians 14:16 shows that the customary Amen was already an institution by the 50s AD.
A recurring thematic pattern in a body of literature. The sword coming from the mouth in Revelation 1:16 is almost a topos.
An archer’s bow, possibly a Scythian loanword and the bow of the ephebe’s citizenship training. In the Septuagint it covers bow and quiver together, so arrows are assumed (Revelation 6:2).
Catching alive. Luke uses this rescue verb at Luke 5:10 (“you will be catching men”), part of a reading of Luke 5 that ties the deep water to the Gentile mission.
Truth or faithfulness.
Living creature. John uses this term, instead of cherub or seraph, for the four eye-filled beings around the throne, blending Ezekiel’s cherubim with Isaiah’s six-winged seraphim (Revelation 4:6-8).
Misery, toil, or trouble.
Integrity or blamelessness.
To save, deliver, or give victory.
Blessed or happy, often rendered “O the happiness of…” It means settled well-being more than a momentary blessing, and the word links Psalms 1 and 2 (Psalm 1:1; 2:12).
Discipline, correction, or instruction.
To vow or make a solemn promise.
An ear of grain, or a flowing stream.
To strike, smite, or defeat.
A consecrated or separated one.
Wonderful, or beyond understanding.
A riddle, enigma, or dark saying.
Jawbone.
To call or cry out.
To shave.
To remember.
An idol or graven image.
A priestly garment, or an object used in worship.
Inheritance.
To go into exile, or to be revealed.
To play the harlot or be unfaithful.
War or battle.
A foolish or disgraceful act.
To regret, grieve, or be comforted.
To draw near.
To possess or to dispossess.
Canaanite.
To weep.
To cry out.
Lightning.
Prophet or prophetess.
Altar.
Song.
Camp.
Horn.
To return or repent.
Faithful or trustworthy.
To say, also glossed as “word.”
To possess, create, or acquire.
A mighty man of valor, or of wealth.
Salvation or deliverance.
Beginning.

Father: head of the corporate household who determines standing and allocates inheritance, and a patron who speaks for his client in the city gate. It also names God as protective, compassionate father (Matthew 6:9).
Destruction, or the place of destruction. It is an Old Testament synonym for Sheol (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11), personified in Revelation as the angel king of the abyss (Revelation 9:11).
How long? The cry of the lament psalms and of the covenant plaintiff for the verdict to be carried out (Psalm 79:5; Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12; Revelation 6:10).
My Lord. The title was read aloud in place of the divine Name, which is why English Bibles print LORD.
Lords. A plural noun of majesty, used both of the one God and of Abraham.
To love (Strong’s H157).
Ram, and metaphorically a leader or ruler. It is the root behind the reading ʾelîm, “rulers,” in Psalm 58:1, which Dahood reads as “rams,” that is, leaders.
Eye. The same word means sparkle or gleam (Ezekiel 1:4, 16), which is star language and a key to the astral reading of the eye-filled creatures (Ezekiel 1:17-18; Revelation 4:6).
Continual, never running out. It is the Old Syriac rendering of epiousios in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:11).
To be firm, reliable, or established. It is the root of emunah and of Amen.
People of the land: the common Jews not aligned with any sect. They were Jesus’s primary audience and were scorned by the Pharisees.
In a courtroom sense, to testify against. Naomi uses it in her legal complaint that Yahweh has testified against her (Ruth 1:21).
Meek or humble. It is used of Moses as power held under authority (Numbers 12:3).
The first-person pronoun “I,” used in the prologue to the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2). Whether it is genuinely more emphatic than ani is an open question.
Guilt offering. It was eaten by priests only and counted most holy (Leviticus 7:1-7).

The ten words or sayings, the Hebrew name for the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5). The name reflects treaty language instead of the term mitzvot, and “Decalogue” is the Greek form of this phrase.
Canaanite fertility goddess or goddesses, a consort figure to Baal. Israel put them away in covenant renewal (1 Samuel 7:3-4).

To work or serve. Paired with shamar in Genesis 2:15 it forms the priestly service word pair, so Adam’s task is priestly service in sacred space more than farm work, as Walton argues (Genesis 2:15; Numbers 3:7-8).
To separate or divide. Leviticus 20:25 uses it both for separating clean from unclean animals and for Israel’s separation from the peoples (Leviticus 10:10; 20:25-26).
To purge, burn, or consume. It is the expiatory verb in “purge the evil from your midst,” framing execution as communal cleansing (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7).
To create. Walton argues it concerns assigning functions, like “creating a committee,” more than producing material, and reads Genesis 1:1 as a functional heading (compare Hebrews 11:3).
Very fat. Eglon’s obesity is a marker of status and a deliberate humiliation in the story (Judges 3:17).
The preposition “in.” Heiser reads it in Genesis 1:26 as beth essentiae, “as” the image, indicating role instead of location.

The Old Testament land chaos monster, Leviathan’s companion on land (Job 40:15-24), rendered thērion in the Septuagint. In 2 Baruch 29 this day-five creature is served as food at the end-time banquet, and it stands behind the land beast of
“In the day,” functioning idiomatically as “when” in Genesis 2:4. Critics say this idiom does not prove a flexible use of the numbered days of Genesis 1.
“In the Wilderness,” the Hebrew title of the book of Numbers.
Son. As an idiom, ben denotes belonging to a category, not literal descent.
Sons of Israel. It is the Masoretic reading of Deuteronomy 32:8, which Tov labels an anti-polytheistic alteration and anachronistic at Babel.

Sons of God. The phrase clusters around the heavenly court and works as a near synonym for the hosts of heaven (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7). It is a strong reading for Genesis 6:1-4, though not airtight, since humans can occasionally be called sons
A variant form of bene elohim, “sons of God,” discussed by Heiser in connection with Deuteronomy 32:8. The phrase also appears in Psalm 29:1 and Psalm 89:6.
Sons of the Most High, a phrase from the vocabulary of the divine council (Psalm 82:6).
In the beginning. It is the opening word of Genesis and the Hebrew title of the book (Genesis 1:1).
“House of God.” In the Old Testament it names the tabernacle or Temple as the single site of God’s dwelling. It was applied to church buildings only after AD 70, especially after Constantine.
“House of Mercy.” The pool by the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem, originally used for washing sacrificial animals and later a syncretistic healing shrine, possibly of Eshmun (John 5:2).

A grammatical use of the Hebrew preposition beth meaning “as” or “in the capacity of.” It is the pivot for reading “in our image” as “as our image” in Genesis 1:26. Joüon-Muraoka confirms the usage at Exodus 18:4 (see also Psalm 146:5).

Balaam, the Old Testament false prophet. Rabbinic tradition explained his name as bala’-‘am (“consumes the people”) or ba’al-‘am (“rules the people”), and he became proverbial for the false teacher who leads believers into compromise (Numbe
“House of bread.” An ironic setting for the famine that opens the book of Ruth (Ruth 1:1).
Benjamin, meaning “son of the right hand.” The name is ironic, since the tribe produced famous left-handed warriors (Judges 3:15; 20:16).

A blessing added to the synagogue prayers that included a curse on sectarians and heretics. It formed part of the exclusion of Christians from synagogues after AD 70, though its dating and target are debated.
To cling or cleave. It is the same verb used in Genesis 2:24, so Ruth’s clinging to Naomi carries marriage-grade covenant language (Ruth 1:14).
“Grain.” It is possibly the strongest etymology for the name Dagon, as a grain or plow god (1 Samuel 5).

The principal Philistine god, and father of Baal in Ugaritic myth. His name’s etymology is unresolved: dag (fish), dagan (grain), and a storm root have all been proposed, and the popular fish-god idea is not established (1 Samuel 5).
To seek or to interpret. It is the root of the word midrash.
“Likeness.” It is paired with tselem (image) in Genesis 1:26, but the two are not strict synonyms.
“Way.” In Psalm 1 it means an entire manner of living and its moral direction, beyond a literal path (Psalm 1:1, 6).

The foundation stone of the Temple, a tradition recorded in Mishnah Yoma 5.2. Bailey and Jeremias see it invoked, together with Isaiah 28:16, in Luke’s builder who builds on the rock, though Snodgrass disagrees (Luke 6:48).
“Calf” or young bull. It may be a wordplay in the name of Eglon, the fat king who is slaughtered like a calf (Judges 3:12).
“One.” In the Shema it affirms the uniqueness of Yahweh and does not deny that other elohim exist (Deuteronomy 6:4).
The generic Semitic word for “god.” When God identifies himself, he never leaves it bare but attaches a qualifying word to it.
“I AM.” The self-existent Name God gives at the burning bush, which carries no category word (Exodus 3:14).
“Thousand,” or possibly a small military unit. The second sense bears on numbers of casualties that seem inflated (1 Samuel 4:10).
“El Most High.” It is a ranking title, which is meaningless unless lower elohim exist (Deuteronomy 32:8).
Eliakim, “God will raise up” (from El and qum). He is the steward in Isaiah 22 given the key of David, read as a type of the risen Christ (Isaiah 22:20 to 22; Revelation 3:7).

Either “gods” (plural of el) or “rulers, mighty ones” (from ayil, “ram”). Broyles documents the two being confused at Psalm 29:1, Psalm 89:6, and Ezekiel 32:21, which bears on the reading of Psalm 58:1.
“My God is king.” The irony is that he leaves the land for Moab (Ruth 1:2).

“Most High.” The Dictionary of Deities and Demons does not speak with one voice on it: its El/Elyon article favors Elyon as Yahweh, while Parker’s article on the sons of God treats Elyon as a separate high god (Deuteronomy 32:8 to 9).
Elizabeth, meaning “My God is an oath” or “God of fullness” (Luke 1:5). Together with Zechariah (“Yahweh remembers”), the names combine into the meaning of John (“Yahweh is gracious”).
“The Everlasting El.” It describes God as un-originated, which no created elohim can be.
“El Almighty.” A qualified form of God’s self-identification (Genesis 35:11).
“Counsel” or “plan” (construct form ʿăṣat). In Psalm 33:10 Yahweh frustrates the counsel of the nations, meaning human political scheming, not the divine council (Psalm 33:10 to 11).
“Woman of valor” or “noble woman.” It is Boaz’s term for Ruth, the same phrase used in Proverbs 31:10 (Ruth 3:11).

“Hebrew servant.” Closer to an indentured servant, entered through debt or restitution for theft, and protected by seventh-year release, the Sabbath year, and Jubilee, with provision on release (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15; Leviticus 25).
“Stone of help.” Samuel’s memorial stands at the place where the ark had been lost, the same ground with the opposite outcome (1 Samuel 7:12; 4:1).
“Man of God” or “God is my strength.” The angel of Daniel 8 and 9 who announces the births of John and Jesus (Daniel 8:16; 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26).
“Coriander” (Coriandrum sativum), the word used to describe manna (HALOT 1612; Exodus 16:31; Numbers 11:7).
To revile or reproach. A concrete honor-attack verb used of insult directed at God.
The Garden of Eden, rendered “garden of luxuries” in the Septuagint (Genesis 2:8).
“Oil press,” the source of the name Gethsemane. Jesus enters the press to undergo the deepest crushing, and oil is the blessing produced through crushing (Matthew 26:36).

“Valley of Hinnom,” the source of the Greek gehenna. It was the site of child sacrifice to Molech and Baal, desecrated by Josiah, and became the image of final fiery judgment (2 Kings 23:10; Isaiah 66:24).
“Mighty warrior.” It is how Jephthah is introduced, immediately qualified as the son of a prostitute (Judges 11:1).
“Mighty men” or warriors, the term used in Genesis 6:4 (Genesis 6:4).
The sciatic sinew. It is the only dietary law grounded in a narrative memory, Jacob’s injured hip (Genesis 32:32).
“Nation.” An ethnolinguistic people group defined by common ancestry, language, territory, and culture, unlike a modern political nation-state (Genesis 10 to 11).
“Kid,” a young goat. It is the word the fertility-ritual reading of the kid-in-milk law needs, yet it differs from the text’s gd by a yod that is not there (Exodus 23:19).

To meditate in the sense of muttering: low, repeated recitation of a memorized text aloud, often while the hands were busy. In Psalm 2 the nations do it to emptiness (Psalm 1:2; 2:1; Isaiah 31:4; Joshua 1:8).
“The man.” Isaiah 14:16 calls the fallen figure of the taunt a man (Isaiah 14:16).
“Walk.” In the hithpael it denotes habitual walking, as in “walk with God” said of Enoch, Noah, and Abraham, one of the canon’s deepest relational images (Genesis 5:24; 6:9; 17:1).
Praise as exuberant boasting or celebration, one end of the biblical range of praise words.
To be gracious, to bend down in mercy. It is the root of the names John, Hannah, and Ananias (Luke 1:13).
Milk. It shares its consonants with chelev (fat), an easy vocabulary trap, and one speculative proposal revocalizes it as fat in the law against boiling a kid in its mother’s milk (Exodus 23:19).
“The revealed things,” which belong to us and our children and are tied to obedience to the Torah (Deuteronomy 29:29).
“The hidden things” or secret things, which belong to the LORD. The contrast in the verse is hidden versus revealed, not earthly versus heavenly (Deuteronomy 29:29).
To dig. One Hebrew verb covers both digging soil and digging for truth (searching out), a link treated as suggestive rather than proof.
To reproach or taunt. An honor-attack verb used of reviling God.
“Mount of assembly” (Isaiah 14:13). Read this way, Armageddon points to Zion and not to Megiddo, which is a plain with no mountain (Revelation 16:16).
Pharaoh’s “magicians”: sacred scribes and wise men with real, demonic power, not mere illusionists (Exodus 7:22; 8:7; 8:19).
To intend or plan. Genesis 50:20 uses it for both the brothers’ evil intent and God’s good intent in a single sentence (Genesis 50:20).
“Bridegroom,” one who enters into covenant and is joined to another (Exodus 4:25 to 26).
“Bridegroom of blood.” A phrase unique to this passage: Zipporah’s declaration that through the blood of circumcision Moses is bound by covenant (Exodus 4:25 to 26).
The sin offering. Its meat was eaten only by the priests, in the holy place (Leviticus 6:24 to 30).
In rabbinic law, the formal warning required before a capital conviction, which the offender had to acknowledge.
A study partnership of peers who spar over the text. Partners are honest enough to say “I don’t know,” argue the text, and welcome disagreement as the path to truth (Proverbs 27:17).

“Shining one” in Isaiah 14:12, rendered “Lucifer” in Jerome’s Latin Vulgate of the late 4th century. The reading is contested (possibly a waning luminary) and has a Ugaritic backdrop in the dawn god Shahar (Isaiah 14:12).

“Shining one, son of dawn” or “day star, son of dawn.” It appears once, in a taunt against the king of Babylon, with parallels to the Ugaritic Shahar and Athtar. Jerome rendered helel as lucifer, but it is not a name for Satan (Isaiah 14:12

Sacrificial fat, the hard suet around the organs, which was the LORD’s portion and burned first. Eli’s sons took meat before it was burned (1 Samuel 2:15-16; Leviticus 3:16-17; 7:23). Not to be confused with chalav (milk). One speculative r
“Sword.” Ehud’s was likely a short sword of bronze or iron, 18 to 24 inches long (Judges 3:16).
Devotion to destruction in holy war. It is a bounded category, not a template for warfare (Deuteronomy 20; Joshua 6:18; 7).

“Riddle.” In the ancient Near East a riddle was a wisdom contest testing privileged access to hidden knowledge, separating the wise from the ordinary. The plural ḥîdôt means “dark sayings” (Judges 14:12 to 18; Proverbs 1:6; Ezekiel 17:2; 1

The hithpael of halak, “to walk about.” A rare form used of God walking in Eden and walking among his people in the tabernacle and temple (Genesis 3:8; Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 23:15; 2 Samuel 7:6 to 7).
Aramaic for “debt,” a word that also means sin. It lies behind “forgive us our debts” in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12).
“I caused you to go out,” a hiphil verb form. It is Yahweh’s self-identification in the prologue to the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2).

“To know.” Paired with tov and ra’ (good and bad), it denotes the capacity to discern and judge between them, not omniscience or sexual maturity. Children lack it, kings need it, and the old lose it (Genesis 2:17; 3:5; Deuteronomy 1:39; 1 K
To praise or give thanks, associated with extended hands. It is part of the Hebrew range of praise words.

The idiom “knowing good and evil,” found in about five passages, denoting the capacity to discern: children lack it, kings need it, and the elderly lose it. It refers to a royal and judicial wisdom prerogative known across the ancient Near
A rare, older verb meaning “shine,” preserved in the Masoretic Text of Isaiah 13:10. The Dead Sea Isaiah scribe replaced it with the common ya’iru (Isaiah 13:10).
“The elohim who is Yahweh,” the divine Name fused to the category word.
A common later verb meaning “shine,” substituted by the Dead Sea Isaiah scribe for the older yahellu (Isaiah 13:10).
“To howl.” A minority view reads the consonants of hêlēl in Isaiah 14:12 as an imperative of this verb (“Howl, son of the morning!”), but it fails on parallelism (Ezekiel 21:12; Isaiah 14:12).
“The sea,” the chaos-sea and domain of Leviathan and Rahab. Its abolition in Revelation 21:1 means chaos undone and Eden restored (Mark 4:41; Isaiah 27:1).
“Right” (the right hand or side), the power hand. Facing east, it was linked with the south, the favorable, sunward direction (Psalm 110:1).
Jacob, the root of the English name James. The name carries the wrestle at the Jabbok, the limp, and the pattern of wound and blessing (Genesis 32).
“Heights of the north,” Baal’s cosmic mountain Zaphon, applied polemically to Zion. The phrase is theology, not geography (Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 14:13).
“The fatherless” or orphan. The fatherless were the model of those needing the community’s protection, since the absence of a father was a category of crisis.

Aramaic for “time,” as in Daniel’s “time, times, and half a time.” The figure equals three and a half years, 42 months, or 1,260 days, and is the Danielic backbone of Revelation 11 to 12 (Daniel 7:25; 12:7; Revelation 12:14).
Beloved of Yahweh. The name God gave Solomon through Nathan, part of a biblical pattern of names given by God (2 Samuel 12:24-25).
Yahweh saves. The name of Joshua, and in its shorter form Yeshua the name of which Jesus is the Greek form, linking Deuteronomy to the Gospels (Joshua 1:1).
Inclination or intent, used of the evil inclination. The Qumran text 4Q422 attributes it to Adam, borrowing it from Genesis 6:5 and 8:21, though Genesis 3 does not use it.
The evil inclination. In Second Temple Judaism it was treated almost as a personal force, which forms background to the way Paul personifies sin.
No glory, or the glory has departed. The name given to Phinehas’s son when the ark was captured, marking the low point of 1 Samuel (1 Samuel 4:21-22).

The personal name of Israel’s God, rendered LORD in small capitals in most English Bibles. It marks his self-existent, unshared identity (Exodus 3:14-15, Isaiah 42:8). The standard count is 6,828 occurrences (Strong’s H3068 plus H3069), whi
Yahweh of hosts. The title presents Yahweh as commander of the heavenly armies.
Yahweh is gracious. The Hebrew form of John, from the root chanan. It is the first name God gives after roughly 400 years of prophetic silence (Luke 1:13).
Day. The word is flexible in meaning: Genesis 2:4 uses it for the whole creation week, which is used in old-earth arguments that the days of Genesis 1 need not be 24-hour days.
Man of God. Used of the unnamed prophet who delivers the first judgment oracle against Eli’s house (1 Samuel 2:27).

Watchers, literally wakeful ones. The Aramaic term used in Daniel 4 (its only Old Testament occurrence) and in 1 Enoch 6 for the rebel angels. Its link with the Akkadian maṣṣarē runs through the apkallu concept as a match in meaning, not a
Mighty man of valor. The title given to Gideon as a warrior (Judges 6:12) and applied to Boaz as a man mighty in character (Ruth 2:1).
Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. The threefold cry of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:3, known as the trisagion.
Wing, and also the corner or edge of a garment. It describes refuge under Yahweh’s wings (Ruth 2:12), and spreading one’s garment over a woman was a formal act of betrothal (Ruth 3:9, Ezekiel 16:8).

Cutting off from the people. Its meaning is debated (death by God’s hand, banishment, or excommunication), with the evidence leaning toward divine action distinct from execution by a court (Leviticus 7:20-27).
Aromatic cane, an ingredient in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23). Sula Benet claimed it was cannabis, a view more defensible than Allegro’s theories but still contested.

Heavy. Eli was heavy (1 Samuel 4:18), one of only two purely literal physical uses in the Hebrew Bible, and the same word describes Yahweh’s heavy hand on the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:6). Related to kavod, glory: Eli’s false weight contrasts
A prefixed preposition meaning as or like, found in the phrase after our likeness (Genesis 1:26).
The Writings, the third division of the Hebrew Bible: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Ruth, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah, and Chronicles (Luke 24:44).

Kidneys, occurring about 30 times. Used in parallel with the heart as the seat of conscience, deep feeling, and sometimes reasoning, so that hearts and kidneys is an idiom for the innermost person. A neat split of heart for thought and kidn

Those who are taught; as a noun, pupils or disciples. The Servant has the tongue of the taught, his ear awakened morning by morning, so he is taught what and how to speak each day (Isaiah 50:4, 8:16, 54:13).
To lodge or spend the night. The same verb as Ruth’s vow in Ruth 1:16, used again by Boaz as he guards her honor (Ruth 3:13).

Leviathan, the sea chaos monster of the Old Testament, the twisting serpent, equivalent to Ugaritic Yam (Isaiah 27:1). It is paired with Behemoth in Job 40-41, and Jewish tradition says it was made on day five and will be destroyed and eate
Not my people. The symbolic name of Hosea’s son (Hosea 1:9), part of the un-peopling and re-peopling theme that stands behind the Spirit’s restoration of God’s people in Zechariah 4:6.
Messengers, the usual word for angels. It names a task, not a type of being, and no passage gives the mal’akim wings, though cherubim and seraphim have them.
Kingdom of priests. Israel’s calling to serve as priestly mediators (Exodus 19:6), applied to the church in Revelation 1:6.
Wealth. Kenneth Bailey finds it in a wordplay with amen and emunah in Luke 16:9-13.
Lord. The usual Aramaic substitute for the divine name.
Bitter. The name Naomi asks to be called when she returns to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:20).
A tenth, or tithe. The king’s tenth in 1 Samuel 8:15, 17 uses the same word as the Levitical tithe, so the tenth that once confessed Yahweh’s rule now funds a human king.
Proverb or parable, and also a taunt song or mocking funeral dirge. Isaiah 14 is a mašal aimed directly at the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4).
The chief dark power in the book of Jubilees, called chief of the spirits and ruler of the demons, the same title the scribes use in Mark 3:22.
Death. The same word as Ugaritic Môt, the Canaanite death deity who devours gods and humans, and the personification behind Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18, Hosea 13:14, Isaiah 5:14).
King of the kings of kings. A stacked title that makes a courtroom claim against ruling powers, seen and unseen.
Chariot, used of the divine throne chariot of Ezekiel 1, above which Ezekiel sees a human form called the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:26-28).
Covering his feet, a euphemism for relieving oneself (Judges 3:24).
From the house of slaves. In the opening of the Ten Commandments, Israel is brought out of Egypt to serve a new master (Exodus 20:2).
Interpretation, from darash, to seek or interpret. It names both a method of interpretation and a kind of text: a story-form retelling that still affirms a real event.
Grain offering. A token portion was burned and the rest went to the priests (Leviticus 2, 6:14-18).

Sectarians or heretics (singular min), a rabbinic term. Who is meant varies by passage and period, sometimes Jewish Christians and sometimes not, so it should not be glossed simply as Jewish Christians.
Sanctuary or holy place, used for example of the oak at Shechem (Genesis 12:6).
Commandments. The Decalogue’s own name for itself is devarim, words, which sets it apart from the mitzvot.
