Betrothal pledge or bride price. The six measures of barley Boaz gives Ruth were likely a down payment of this kind (Ruth 3:15-17).
Dying you shall die. The phrase means becoming subject to death, not instant execution, with banishment from the tree of life as the sentence taking effect (Genesis 2:17).
To fall. The traditional derivation of Nephilim, which yields the reading fallen ones (Genesis 6:4).
Giant. Heiser proposes this Aramaic word as the source of Nephilim, against the Hebrew naphal, to fall (Genesis 6:4).
To touch, reach, or strike. It can mean touched or confronted in a physical, immediate, and life-threatening sense.

Serpent. The root carries three senses (serpent, deception or divination, and to shine), so the figure in Genesis 3 can be read as deceiver, shining one, and serpentine throne guardian (Genesis 3:1, Ezekiel 28:12-17). The lexical layers are
Fiery serpent, the two words appearing together (Numbers 21:6, Deuteronomy 8:15).
Pleasant or sweet. The name of Ruth’s mother-in-law (Ruth 1:2).
A phrase from Psalm 23:3. Snodgrass reads it as refresh me or rescue me, while Kenneth Bailey reads it as bring me back or cause me to repent.

To drill, bore, or pierce. The meaning develops from drill to designate, then designate as bad, then blaspheme. In Leviticus 24, piercing the Name is an utterance that penetrates the divine sphere (Kamionkowski) and carries the death penalt
To take up the name of YHWH in vain: attaching God’s name to something empty or false (Exodus 20:7). It separates acting in God’s name from simply acting as a Christian.
Let us make. A plural cohortative verb form in Genesis 1:26.
The form that would be needed to read Nephilim as those who fell. Its absence in Genesis 6:4 supports Heiser’s reading of Nephilim as giants.
Bronze or copper, the shining metal, from the same root as nachash (Numbers 21:9).
A setting or mounting for gemstones, a jeweler’s term. In Ezekiel 28:13 (KJV pipes) it fits the list of nine precious stones.
Carcass, an animal that died of itself. It could be given to a resident alien or sold to a foreigner, showing that the law is about Israel, not the meat itself (Deuteronomy 14:21).
The Prophets, the second division of the Hebrew Bible: the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve).
The form that would be needed to read Nephilim as those who fall upon others. Its absence in Genesis 6:4 supports Heiser’s reading of Nephilim as giants.
Foreigner (feminine nokriyyâ). In Ruth 2:10 it plays on hakkir, to notice, from the same root nkr.

Familiar spirit (KJV). Originally a ritual pit for contacting underworld spirits, later the spirit itself or the medium (Leviticus 19:31, 20:27, 1 Samuel 28). A link to ancestor worship is possible, and the etymology is contested.
Servant, possibly short for Obadiah, servant of Yahweh. Ruth 4:17 leaves open whether he is servant of God or of Naomi.
Those who pass over: spirits of the dead crossing to the underworld. It names the burial valley of Gog (Ezekiel 39:11) and echoes Ugaritic cult-of-the-dead language.

Tumors or swellings struck on the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:6, 9). The mainstream reading is bubonic plague, given the golden mice. Heiser, citing finds at Ashkelon, reads it as a strike on fertility aimed at Dagon’s domain.
Burnt offering, burned entirely and eaten by no one (Leviticus 1).
Wheels, the wheels of Ezekiel’s throne vision (Ezekiel 1).
To meet or encounter (Strong’s H6298). It is the verb in Exodus 4:24, where the hostility comes from the following clause, not from the verb.
To be separated or distinct. Gilbrant proposes it as a third possible derivation for Nephilim (Genesis 6:4).
Court. The KJV translators could not translate it in 1611 and so transliterated it (1 Chronicles 26:18).

The Syriac equivalent of Greek prosopon. For Syriac speakers it meant that which presents itself to observation, while in Rome and Alexandria the corresponding term meant an individual subject. This gap in vocabulary lies behind the Nestori
Invalid or unfit, used of a Torah scroll disqualified by a scribal error.
Mr. So-and-So. A rhyming non-name for the nearer redeemer in Ruth 4:1, deliberately withholding his name.
Fruit. Genesis never says the fruit was an apple (Genesis 3:6).

Interpretation (plural pesharim). At Qumran, a running commentary that quotes a line of text, says its interpretation is, and then applies it. Pesharim were written only on Hebrew Bible books, 1 Enoch, and the Temple Scroll.
Foul thing or refuse: sacrificial meat eaten past its allowed time, on the third day (Leviticus 7:18).
To make light or small, to treat as weightless, and so to curse. Cursing God in Leviticus 24:15 brings bearing sin, not death, a different act from naqav.
Reed, related to the Semitic kanna. A reed used as a measuring rod lies behind the word canon.

To shine or be radiant. It shares its consonants (q-r-n) with the noun for horn, qeren, which is why the Vulgate described Moses’ face as horned (Exodus 34:29-35). A fluent reader may have heard a pun on closeness to God.

A village ceremony of cutting off a son who lost family property among Gentiles (also spelled kezazah). Kenneth Bailey, following Rengstorf in a modest form, sees it behind the father running to meet the prodigal son, while Snodgrass finds
Holy ones, the members of the heavenly council (Psalm 89:5, 7, Job 5:1). In Proverbs 9:10 the plural refers to Yahweh as a plural of majesty.

A Syriac term read as individual by Chalcedonians but as a set of characteristics by the Church of the East. Whether speaking of two qnome in Christ is compatible with Chalcedon remains an open question.

Bad or evil: the comprehensive opposite of tov, covering moral evil, poor quality, harm, misfortune and ugliness. Hebrew does not split “bad” from “evil”; the word names whatever diminishes life and relationship (Deuteronomy 30:15; Isaiah 4
To see or look. With the preposition bə it means “look at” or “look upon.” Keil and Delitzsch read it at Beth-shemesh as foolish staring, not necessarily looking inside the ark (1 Samuel 6:19).
The land chaos-monster, also used as a name for Egypt. Rahab is Behemoth’s counterpart and is paired with Leviathan in chaos contexts (Psalm 87:4; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9).
Firmament: the solid sky of Israel’s ancient cosmology. Genesis 1 retains it without correction (Genesis 1:6-8).

Foot (dual raglayim, feet). It can be a euphemism for the genitals, which makes the threshing-floor vocabulary of Ruth deliberately double-edged, though in Exodus 4:25 Moses’ actual feet are likely what was touched (Ruth 3:4-8; Isaiah 7:20)
Fragrance or scent.
Beginning. Walton reads it in Genesis 1:1 as an initial period rather than a first instant.

Dispute or lawsuit, especially a covenant lawsuit. The legal term signals a divine courtroom scene where God indicts his people for breach of covenant, with Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28-29 as the basis (Micah 6:1-2).
Maggot. It parallels tôlaʿath in the language of decay, connoting death and corruption (Isaiah 14:11; Job 25:6).
To laud or commend loudly. One of the Hebrew words for praise.
Hosts or armies, as in Yahweh Sabaoth (Tseva’ot). The title presents God as commander of the heavenly armies and appears more than 280 times.
Rest. Walton and Heiser understand God’s rest as God taking up residence to rule, and the seventh day lacks the evening-morning closing formula (Genesis 2:2-3; Hebrews 4).
A divine title usually rendered “the Almighty.” Naomi uses it in her bitterest accusations (Ruth 1:20-21), and it may be an epithet of El as chief of the divine council.
Divine beings in the Deir Alla inscription about Balaam, who send him a night vision and negotiate with Shgr and El in a divine-council scene. The inscription is background for Numbers 22-24.
Doubt.
To dwell. It is the root of Shekinah.
To lie down. In Ruth 3:4 it is a charged verb that Boaz avoids in favor of lin.

To ask or request, with a base meaning that may lean toward “demand” (Gerleman). Senses include request, asking after someone’s welfare, and inquiring of an oracle. It drives the wordplay on Hannah, Samuel and Saul, including the 1 Samuel 1
To keep or guard. Paired with ‘avad it describes priestly guarding of sacred space, so Adam is commissioned as a priest in the garden sanctuary (Genesis 2:15; Numbers 3:7-8).
Prince. In Daniel 10 it names angelic princes over nations, locked in conflict.

Fiery or burning one, from a root meaning “to burn.” Outside Isaiah 6 its five uses name a fiery or flying serpent, and the seraphim of Isaiah 6 are winged serpentine beings with an Egyptian winged-uraeus background (Isaiah 6:2; Numbers 21;
Flying serpent (Isaiah 14:29; 30:6).
An ordinary Hebrew noun meaning “adversary.” The angel opposing Balaam is a satan in the same sense as the figure in Job’s prologue (Numbers 22:22; 1 Chronicles 21:1).

To plant, deliberately and with irrigation. In Psalm 1:3 the participle shatul, “planted” or “transplanted,” suggests someone else placed the tree there. The same root appears in Jeremiah 17:8, and which text depends on the other is unresol
Saul’s name, meaning “asked for.” The wordplay is that Saul is the king Israel demanded (1 Samuel 9).
Rod, the shepherd’s rod of Proverbs (Proverbs 13:24). The saying “spare the rod, spoil the child” comes from Butler’s Hudibras, not the Bible.
A demon or foreign god; the plural is shedim (Deuteronomy 32:17).
Scroll or book. It is the word used when God first commands Moses to write a memorial (Exodus 17:14).

A post-biblical term, from shakhan (“to dwell”), for the visible manifestation of God’s presence (Exodus 40:34-35). The glory departed the temple in Ezekiel 10-11 and never returned to the Second Temple.

The peace or fellowship offering, a shared sacrifice in which God receives the fat, the priest the breast and thigh, and the worshiper the meal. It expresses peace and wholeness (shalom) as a holy covenant meal (Leviticus 3; 7:11-21, 31-34;
A word in the Psalms whose meaning is still uncertain. It is probably a musical notation.

The imperative “hear” or “listen,” and the name of the prayer beginning at Deuteronomy 6:4-5. The verb carries obedience as well as hearing. By the Second Temple period it was recited daily with the Ten Commandments (m. Tamid 5:1), and Jesu
Detestable thing. It is stronger than tame’ and is used for water creatures and swarming things (Leviticus 11:10-12).
The Community Rule of Qumran (1QS). Its columns 3-4 lay out the doctrine of the Two Spirits.
To put a name, as in Numbers 6:27, “so shall they put my name upon the people of Israel.” It is the Old Testament language of bearing God’s name, which the mark of the beast parodies.
A homograph (HALOT) meaning either locusts and small field pests or a cow’s teat. In Psalm 50:11 (ziz sadai) it refers to ordinary wild animals, not a cosmic creature (Psalm 80:13).
Left, as in the left hand or left side. It carries inauspicious connotations.
The council of Yahweh (Jeremiah 23:18, 22).
Judges or deliverers, the Hebrew title of the book of Judges. It lies behind the alternative name “Book of Deliverers,” which stresses their role as military deliverers.

The Feast of Tabernacles, celebrated with palm branches (Leviticus 23:40). It celebrates deliverance and God dwelling with his people, which stands behind the palms of the multitude in Revelation 7:9 (Revelation 21:3).

The hem, skirt or train of a garment. In Isaiah 6:1 the train of the Lord’s robe fills the temple, and the Septuagint substitutes “glory” for “train.” There is no evidence for the claim that kings sewed conquest swatches onto their trains (
Samuel’s name. Rearranging its consonants yields “asked from Yahweh,” which Hoffner treats as artistry, not corruption (1 Samuel 1:20).
The small crownlets drawn on certain letters in Torah scrolls, a detail of scribal craft.
Lamb, servant or child (compare talitha). The range opens a Servant reading of “Lamb” in John 1:29, drawing on Isaiah 53:7.
Disciple or student.
Unclean or ritually impure; the standard term (Leviticus 11).
The daily, continual sacrifice. In Luke 1:10 the multitude prayed outside while incense was offered during it.
The last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, shaped like an X or cross in paleo-Hebrew. It is the mark on the foreheads of the faithful remnant in Ezekiel 9:4, behind the seal of Revelation 7:3.

Small leather cases holding slips of Scripture, bound to the arm and head in Jewish prayer and also called phylacteries. The practice is read out of Deuteronomy 6:8, and over half the tefillin found at Qumran contain the Ten Commandments.
A song or hymn of praise. One of the Hebrew words for praise.
The scribal substitute reading (qere) written in place of ophalim in 1 Samuel 5:6.
Torn: an animal killed by wild beasts, which was to be thrown to the dogs (Exodus 22:31).
In Ezekiel 28:13, better read as a setting or mounting for gemstones. The KJV rendering “tabrets” is a guess, and the claim that Satan invented music rests on that mistranslation.
The starting state of Genesis 1:2, better rendered “unproductive” or “nonfunctional.” Material exists, but order and purpose are missing.

Worm. The same word names the contemptible maggot of decay (parallel to rimmāh) and the prized crimson royal dye (Psalm 22:6; Isaiah 14:11; Isaiah 1:18; Job 25:6). The legend of a “crimson worm” crucifixion cipher has no ancient attestation

“Worm of scarlet,” the standard biblical term for crimson dye. It colored the tabernacle textiles and was used in purification rites (Exodus 25-28; Leviticus 14; Numbers 19). The dye came from the kermes insect, the ancient Near Eastern sou
Generations, or “the account of.” It is the structuring formula of Genesis (Genesis 2:4), which Walton uses to read Genesis 1:1 as a literary introduction.
The sign bound between the eyes in Deuteronomy 6:8, the basis of the tefillin practice.
Good. God declares creation tov, and the question running through Genesis 1-3 is who has the authority to define it (Genesis 3:5; Deuteronomy 30:15).
Thanksgiving, as praise or offering: a recital of God’s acts full of specific content. One of the Hebrew words for praise.
Very good, “good, exceedingly” (Genesis 1:31). It does not mean perfect: the world was good raw material with work left to do.
Righteous one. The Septuagint renders it dikaios, and it belongs to the Old Testament’s covenant vocabulary (Luke 1:6).
Traditionally “rib” in Genesis 2, though it can be read as “side” (Genesis 2:21-22).
“The Branch,” Zechariah’s title for the priest-king Joshua, crowned to build the Temple (Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). It is read as a title of the Messiah.

North, and in mythic geography the cosmic north: Mount Zaphon, Baal’s mountain and the mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13). Gog comes from the heights of the north, and Psalm 48 applies the title to Zion (Ezekiel 38:6, 15; Psalm 48:2).
The host of heaven: the divine assembly (1 Kings 22:19).
To make music or sing praise, with instruments. One of the Hebrew words for praise.
“Yahweh remembers.” In Luke 1:5 the name forms part of a name-poem with Elizabeth and John.
Light. One of the key words of John’s Gospel.
To believe. One of the key words of John’s Gospel.
Father. One of the key words of John’s Gospel.
Son. One of the key words of John’s Gospel.
The Sumerian god of the heavens or sky. One of Uruk’s two great temple complexes, the White Temple, belonged to him.

Mesopotamian semi-divine sages who brought civilization and forbidden skills. The teaching motif attaches to the Watchers of 1 Enoch 8 more than to Genesis, and Sarna reads Genesis 4:17-22 as a silent polemic against crediting culture to su
“Ravings of the apocrypha”: Jerome’s dismissive phrase in his preface to the Pentateuch.
The watery abyss, where the apkallu were created.
The argument or proof section of a classical forensic speech. It is present in Stephen’s speech (Acts 7).
“Noble” or “free”: the Iranian self-designation in Achaemenid inscriptions and the Avesta. It was later hijacked into a racial category.
“Of the Aryans” or “land of the Aryans,” the root of the name Iran (Middle Persian Ērān).
“Athanasius against the world.” Athanasius was exiled five times in 46 years for defending homoousios.

The Venus star-deity who sat on Baal’s vacant throne, proved too small, and stepped down. Isaiah 14:12-15 invokes this myth, sharing six elements with it: ascent, Zaphon, sitting, throne, descent and underworld.
The cosmic axis joining heaven, earth and underworld: the localized point of contact between God and creation. In biblical theology it is Jerusalem or Zion (Genesis 2; Ezekiel 5:5; 28:13-14; 38:12).
A Mesopotamian diviner or seer priest.
Mesopotamian extispicy, the art of divination. It read right and left as major interpretive axes.
“Sons of El,” the assembly of gods in Ugaritic myth. Heiser works from this divine-council background, and the “seventy sons” rests on KTU 1.4 vi 46 (Deuteronomy 32:8).
“Blessed.” The Latin name of Zechariah’s song (Luke 1:67-79).
“You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian.” The Judge’s words to Jerome in his fever dream (Letter 22).
A book with pages bound at one edge. The word originally meant “tree trunk” or “block of wood.” Christians adopted the codex for scripture around AD 100 to 200.
A council of friends and officials who acted as legal consultants around a Roman governor on the tribunal.
“Horned.” Jerome’s Vulgate rendering of Moses’ face in Exodus 34:29, following Aquila’s keratōdēs. His Ezekiel commentary shows he knew the sense was “glorified,” so the choice was deliberate.
“Gourd.” The Old Latin word in Jonah 4:6 that Jerome replaced with hedera (ivy), which caused a riot at Oea.
A righteous sage in Ugaritic texts, a pre-biblical Daniel figure (Ezekiel 14:14).
“The two-horned one.” The Quran’s name for Alexander the Great, reflecting the horned-divinity motif.
A Roman silver coin worth one day’s wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:1-16). A copy of Luke cost around 300 to 500 denarii.
The Latin source of “diet” (via Old French diete). It also gave “Diet” in the sense of an assembly, as in the Diet of Worms, influenced by dies, “day.”
A reconstructed Proto-Indo-European name meaning “Sky Father.” It is the genuine linguistic source behind Zeus, Jupiter, Dyaus and Týr, and survives in weekday names.
“Son of the Divine One,” a title Augustus took after Julius Caesar’s deification and stamped on his coins. The gospels’ “Son of God” is a direct counter-claim.
“House of the heavens.” The temple complex of the goddess Inana at Uruk.
Sumerian for “lord” or “priest,” the title of Uruk’s priest-king. Its pictographic sign is a stack of beveled-rim bowls.
The Sumerian water god, shown enthroned under a canopy on cylinder seals.
Old English for ground or soil (Proto-Germanic erþō). It is the source of “Earth,” with no deity involved.
The temple of Marduk and Zarpanitu in Babylon. This detail comes from Walton rather than Heiser.
Babylon’s ziggurat, distinct from the Esagila temple. Heiser ties it to Babel (Genesis 11), and his argument about Og runs through it.
“Off the cross.” The source of English “excruciating.”
“Outside the church, no salvation.” Its meaning demonstrably shifted between Unam Sanctam (1302) and the Catechism (paragraph 841).
The opening division of a classical forensic speech. Stephen’s defense in Acts 7 has one.
“Outside the order.” A Roman governor proceeding outside the established court procedure, the ordo judiciorum publicorum.
“Servant” or household attendant, someone who could be summoned. It is one sense behind the Geneva and KJV “familiar” spirit.
“Member of the family,” someone intimate with the household, here with the dead. It is one sense behind the KJV’s “familiar” spirit, which never meant “well-known.”
“Let it be.” The Vulgate’s rendering of amen, following the Septuagint’s genoito.
“Cockcrow,” the Roman third night watch. It has been proposed as a horn or bugle signal behind Peter’s cock crow (Mark 14:72), though this is judged less likely.

“Coriander.” In KTU 1.23 line 14 the word was once reconstructed as “kid” to support a Canaanite kid-in-milk fertility ritual, but the line reads closer to “sacrifice coriander with milk” (Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21).
“Glorified.” The meaning Jerome held for Moses’ face in Exodus 34:29, stated alongside “or, as the Hebrew has it, horned.”
“The Hebrew truth.” Jerome’s principle that the Hebrew original has authority over the Greek translation. In practice he often worked through Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion.
“Ivy.” Jerome’s rendering in Jonah 4:6, following Aquila, in place of the Old Latin cucurbita (gourd).
A name in Suetonius’s account of Claudius expelling Jews from Rome in AD 49. Most scholars read it as a garbled reference to Christus, Christ.
The Ugaritic sea-god, a seven-headed sea monster equated with Leviathan (Psalm 74; Isaiah 27:1). Some tie the seven heads of the beast in Revelation 13 to it.
“Deified ancestor.” It heads Ugaritic sacrificial lists and is probably the same kind of thing as the Hebrew ob.
“Right,” the favorable side in Mesopotamian omen literature.
The Sumerian goddess of love and warfare, patron of the Eanna at Uruk. Her symbol, a tall reed bundle with a looped top and streamer, is the sign that writes her name.
The law of retaliation, measure for measure. For perjury the false witness receives the penalty he sought (Deuteronomy 19:16-21), a deterrent structure that is not applied literally.
A certificate issued under Decius (around AD 250) proving that a person had sacrificed. It shows that a loyalty-gated marketplace was not hypothetical (Revelation 13:17).

“Books outside the canon,” read for the edification of the people rather than to confirm church doctrine. The phrase comes from Jiménez’s preface to the Complutensian Polyglot, quoting Jerome’s Preface to the Books of Solomon.

The sea serpent of Ugaritic myth (also written Litan or Litanu), recognizably Leviathan, a chaos beast defeated by Baal. KTU 1.5 i 1-3 is nearly identical to Isaiah 27:1, and Psalm 74:12-17 gives the victory to Yahweh.

“Light-bearer” (lux plus ferre), the ordinary Latin word for the planet Venus. Jerome used it in the Vulgate at Isaiah 14:12, and English later carried it over as a proper name. The Vulgate also uses it in 2 Peter 1:19 for the morning star
“(My soul) magnifies.” The Latin name of Mary’s song (Luke 1:46-55).
A Latin pun on “apple” and “evil” in the Vulgate, the source of the apple tradition in Genesis 3.
“Watchers” or “guardians.” It corresponds in meaning to the Aramaic ʿîrîn (Watchers), though the link between the two is semantic rather than lexical.
The Egyptian concept of cosmic order, maintained by Ra’s daily journey. Darkness represented chaos, the background to the plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21-29).
“Remember you will die.” Compare Psalm 90:12.
“Thousand,” the root of “millennialism,” the same doctrine as the Greek-derived “chiliasm.”

“Mouth-opening,” the ritual that animated idols as divine representatives, also called pīt pî. It invited a god to indwell its statue so the idol could see, hear and receive offerings. It is background for the idea of humans as God’s imager
The Canaanite death god and chief enemy of Baal. He has an enormous, insatiable mouth, dwells in the muddy underworld and carries a scepter.
The narrative or statement-of-facts division of classical forensic rhetoric. Stephen’s speech in Acts 7 includes it.
The established Roman public-court procedure, which a governor could follow or bypass.
“Roman peace,” the period of relative peace enforced by Rome. It made travel safe and helped the gospel spread (Galatians 4:4).
Old Persian region name (modern Fars) behind the Greek Persis, the source of “Persia.”
The concluding division of a forensic speech. Stephen reaches it by Acts 7:51, turning the charges back on his accusers.
The plural of majesty, or royal “we.” It is attested only on nouns (adonim, qedoshim), never undisputedly on verbs or pronouns, so it cannot explain Genesis 1:26.
“Helmeted Preface” (around 391), Jerome’s preface to Samuel and Kings. It lists a 22-book Old Testament and places Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit and 1 and 2 Maccabees among the apocrypha.
“First gospel,” the name for Genesis 3:15, the promise that the woman’s seed will crush the serpent’s head. It is the root of the woman-and-dragon scene in Revelation 12:2, 5.
A Roman citizen’s right of appeal and freedom from torture, which noncitizens lacked. Paul used it (Acts 22:25-29; Acts 25:11).
Wax tablets: wooden boards filled with beeswax, the ancient reusable notebook (Greek deltoi).
“We shall be caught up,” the Vulgate rendering in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 from which English “rapture” comes. The label is a translation artifact one step removed from the Greek text.
The Vulgate-derived Latin behind English “rapture,” rendering the Greek harpazō in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. The word is not in the original Hebrew or Greek.
“To bind fast.” Lactantius’s etymology of religio, favored in Christian usage.
“To re-read, attend to scrupulously.” Cicero’s proposed etymology of religio.
The root of “religion.” Cicero derived it from relegere (to re-read, attend scrupulously), and Lactantius from religare (to bind fast). Christian usage favored religare: religion binds you to God.
Egyptian for “people.” Its wordplay with remyt, “tears,” underlies the myth of humans born from the creator god Ra’s tears. Egyptian creation was divine crafting, with no worm-to-human evolution.
“The fragrance of coriander and purple snails,” a line from the Baal Cycle (CTA 3.ii.2f). The aromatic context shows that gdm is the herb.
Egyptian for “tears,” punned with remetj, “people,” in the Egyptian account of human origins.
“Rider of the clouds,” an epithet of Baal, echoed in Psalm 68:4.
A territorial term that Heiser connects to the Hebrew shedim (Deuteronomy 32:17).
The Ugaritic Rephaim, divine residents of the underworld, paralleled with underworld gods. In the Hebrew Bible the Rephaim become giants and warriors, stripped of divine status.
The dawn god in Ugaritic myth, the backdrop to “son of dawn” in Isaiah 14:12.
The morning greeting clients paid their patron in the Roman patronage system.
“By faith alone.” The doctrine that justification comes by faith as the sole instrument that lays hold of Christ (Romans 3-4).
“Always faithful.” A public commitment maintained under pressure, closer to the Greek pistis than to the modern religious sense of “faith.”
“Scripture alone” as final authority. Tradition keeps a ministerial (serving) role and has no magisterial (ruling) one.
“Glory to God alone.”
“Left,” the unfavorable side in Mesopotamian omen literature.
“Supersubstantial.” Jerome’s rendering of epiousios in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:11), which fed Eucharistic readings.
The Islamic charge that scripture has been corrupted. It originally meant distortion of meaning, and claims of wholesale textual corruption were systematized later (Ibn Hazm, 11th century).
An ancient Near Eastern concept of knowing how to put the world the way it ought to be. Walton uses it to ground “knowing good and evil” (Genesis 2:17) as awareness of what is conducive to order.
Land or ground, the source of “terrestrial,” “subterranean” and “terra firma.” The personified goddess Terra or Tellus Mater came after the word for soil, the reverse of the other planet names.
“Trinity.” The term is reportedly coined by Tertullian.
Scholar or sage (also ummanu): the fully human sages after the flood, distinct from the apkallu.
“One-horned,” from the Septuagint’s monokerōs. The source of English “unicorn.”
“Prince.” It stands behind Beelzebul (“Exalted Baal” or “Baal is prince”), rendered in Greek as archōn, “ruler” (Mark 3:22).
To be fully convinced, fully assured, or completely certain. Romans 4:21: he was fully convinced that God is able to do whatever he promises.
To count, reckon, credit, or take into account. It can also mean to hold a view or regard something a certain way (Louw-Nida 31.1).
To bless.
